About M&M Gutters & Exteriors

Mission Statement

At M&M Gutters and Exteriors, we have built an organization to act as advocates for homeowners. By vertically integrating all exterior trades, our customers can trust their job to be solid from the foundation to the roof.

Our History

M&M Gutters has been in the valley for more than 30 years. We got our start in 1990. The ownership has changed one time. In 2005, Nate Nuttall came on board when his cousin worked here. He started off as an installer. A few months later he became a sales rep which ultimately led to him getting promoted into management.

Then in 2010, the previous owner decided he wanted to retire and Nate purchased the business! He is proud to say he has done everything at the company and he continues to make it part of his regular routine going out to job sites and meeting with customers. And while family brought him to the business, he continues to employ family members. M&M Gutters and Exteriors is a true to their word family business.

Our Core Values

Communication

Communication is the lifeline of our company. It is essential for seamless collaboration and successful project outcomes. We prioritize clear, timely, and transparent communication at every level of our projects. This allows us to become partners in helping to make projects, dreams and hopes a reality for those we come in contact with.

Integrity

Integrity is the cornerstone of our company culture, guiding every decision and action we take. We uphold the highest ethical standards – demonstrating honesty, transparency, and accountability in all our interactions. Our commitment to integrity means that we do what we say we will do, always prioritize the well-being of our clients and employees, and strive to build lasting relationships based on trust and respect. We believe that integrity is non-negotiable and essential for the long-term success and sustainability of our business.

Responsibility

Responsibility stands as the cornerstone of our construction company’s ethos, ingrained deeply within our operations and culture. We believe in shouldering accountability at every stage of our projects, from planning to execution and beyond. Our commitment to responsibility manifests in various forms: ensuring the safety of our workers, doing things the right way and delivering high-quality results that meet or exceed expectations.

Community

Empowering communities through exceptional craftsmanship and sustainable solutions, our company is dedicated to delivering innovative, high-quality projects that enhance lives, foster growth, and build a better future for generations to come. Our commitment to be a positive force in our communities drives us in all the decisions we make.

Adaptability

We embrace innovation and flexibility – responding quickly and effectively to shifting priorities, challenges, and opportunities. Our team is adept at navigating complexities and finding creative solutions to overcome obstacles, ensuring the success of every project. We commit to continually learning, training and innovating the industry. By fostering a culture of adaptability, we stay ahead of industry trends, embrace new technologies, and continuously improve our processes to deliver the highest quality projects.

title: 11 Signs You Need New Windows for Your Home - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
h1: 11 Signs You Need New Windows for Your Home
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
Over time, your windows can show signs of wear and tear, letting you know it’s time for replacement. When these signs show up, you may wonder, “Should I replace my windows? Can I just repair them?” In this blog, we’ll discuss how to know when to replace windows and address other common questions about window replacement.

How Do I Know When to Replace My Windows?

Windows generally last between 15 and 20 years, but how often to replace them depends on the quality of the material and installation. If you notice factors like leaking, fading furniture, drafts, or increasing energy bills, you may be better off with a full-blown replacement.

Here are 11 signs to look for that indicate it’s time to replace your windows.

1. Damage to the Frame and Glass

One of the most obvious ways to know when to replace windows is when there’s visible damage to the frame and glass. Cracks, rot, and warping can compromise the structural integrity, impacting functionality.

2. Water Leaks Through

If you notice water leaking through your windows during rain or storms, it’s a clear sign that the seals have deteriorated. Leaky windows should be replaced because they can lead to water damage and mold.

3. Windows Are Hard to Open or Close

Windows should open and close effortlessly. If they stick or jam, you might need to replace your windows.

4. Loud Outdoor Noise

If outdoor sounds are louder than they used to be, it’s a sign your windows are no longer effectively soundproof. Upgrading to new windows can bring peace and quiet to your home.

5. Windows Are Foggy

Foggy windows indicate a failed seal, allowing moisture to accumulate between the panels. This obstructs your view and reduces your window’s insulation abilities.

6. You See Condensation in the Inside of Your Window

Condensation on the inside of your windows is a sign of poor insulation. Replacing your windows can help prevent this issue.

7. High Energy Bills

Old, inefficient windows can cause higher energy bills. New windows with better insulation can lead to energy savings.

8. Drafts

Feeling drafts around your windows is a clear sign of air leaking. New windows can provide better sealing, improving energy efficiency.

9. Items Near the Windows Are Fading

If you notice your furniture, carpets, or curtains fading, it could be caused by UV rays entering through worn-out windows. Upgrading your windows can protect your belongings.

10. Desire to Increase Your Home Value

Investing in new windows can enhance your home’s overall value. Modern, energy-efficient windows may attract potential buyers.

11. Allergens

If you begin to experience sneezing, itchy, watery eyes, or itchy skin, your windows may be allowing allergens to enter.

Factors Affecting the Lifespan of Your Windows

Before shopping for new windows, it’s essential to understand the factors that affect their lifespan. Here are a few factors to keep in mind:

  • Material: Wood frames are often prone to rotting compared to vinyl and fiberglass frames.
  • Quality: High-quality windows, featuring durable glass and energy-efficient coatings, often have better seals, which can enhance the lifespan of your window.
  • Installation: Poorly insulated windows can lead to air leaks and water damage.
  • Climate: Frequent exposure to harsh snow, rain, and windstorms accelerates window aging.
  • Maintenance: Regularly checking and cleaning your windows can help keep them functioning properly.

Benefits of Replacing Your Windows

    • Decreased energy costs and lower carbon footprint
    • Enhanced insulation for improved indoor comfort
    • A quieter indoor environment with noise reduction
    • Improved safety features
    • Effortless window operation (easy to open and close)
    • Clearer view of the outdoor surroundings
    • Enhanced aesthetics for a modern look
    • Elevated property value

How Much Do New Windows Cost?

If you need new windows, you can expect to pay between $175 and $2,300 per window for replacement. Custom and large windows may cost more.

Should I Replace Every Window at the Same Time?

Windows need to be replaced when you notice any of the ten signs above. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean every window needs to be replaced. You can replace them all if you want a uniform look or prioritize windows based on need and budget.

How Often Do Windows Need to Be Replaced?

Windows have a typical lifespan of 15-20 years. You should replace 20-year-old windows or windows with any of the above-mentioned issues.

When to Replace Windows vs. When to Repair Them

Repairs can be a cost-effective short-term solution for minor issues such as cracks or seal failures, especially for those on a tight budget. However, if windows have extensive damage or are reaching the end of their lifespan, replacement can be a more sensible long-term investment. You should consider replacing your windows if:

  • Your windows are over 20 years old.
  • You want to enhance your home’s resale value.
  • You want to save money on energy bills with energy-efficient windows.
  • You want to improve the look of your home.

What Time of the Year Is the Cheapest to Replace Windows?

Late fall or early winter is typically the least busy time for window replacement, making it the most cost-effective time of year to replace your windows.

Do You Need New Windows?

If any of the above signs sound familiar and you need new windows for your home, trust the professionals at M&M Gutters! We have years of experience delivering exceptional window replacement services. Contact us today to schedule a consultation.

title: 12 Signs You Need a New Roof for Your Home - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
h1: 12 Signs You Need a New Roof for Your Home
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
Most roofs exhibit clear signs when it’s time for replacement, such as missing shingles, leaks, and sagging areas; however, not all signs are immediately apparent. As your home’s first line of defense, your roof endures the relentless impact of sun, rain, snow, and more. Over time, wear and tear accumulate, making it essential to determine when your roof needs to be replaced.

Below, we’ll discuss how to tell if you need a new roof and what to do if it’s time to replace it.

How Do You Know It’s Time to Replace a Roof?

You’ll know it’s time to replace your roof if you see missing or cracked shingles, water damage, sunlight peeking through, or if your roof is over 20 years old. You can always invest in a professional inspection to gain an expert opinion.

Here are the top 11 definite warning signs you need a new roof.

1. Exceeded Its 20-30 Year Lifespan

If your roof is older than 20 to 30 years, it may be time to replace it. The aging process compromises the effectiveness of roofing materials, making your home more susceptible to damage from external elements.

2. Daylight Peeks Through

If you can see sunlight coming through your roof boards, it’s a sure sign that you need a new roof. This indicates potential leaks and suggests that your home is less energy-efficient.

3. Visible Water Damage and Leaks

Water stains inside the attic, on your ceiling, or on your walls are obvious signs that something is wrong with your roof. Persistent leaks can cause more significant damage, like mold and structural issues.

4. Sagging Roof

A sagging roof is a serious structural problem that needs swift attention. It could result from water damage, aging materials, or a compromised foundation.

5. Buckling or Curling Shingles

Shingles that are buckling or curling are no longer providing sufficient protection for your home. Buckling and curling can be caused by weathering, insufficient ventilation, or poor installation. If you notice either of these problems, you should replace your roof shingles.

6. Cracked or Damaged Shingles

One way to tell if a roof needs to be replaced is when there are several cracked or damaged shingles. Weather, heavy impact, inadequate ventilation, and freeze-thaw cycles can cause shingle damage. You should regularly inspect your roof to identify and replace weakened shingles before further damage occurs and you need a whole new roof.

7. Missing Shingles

Missing shingles expose your roof to weather and water, which makes it susceptible to leaks and damage. Quickly replacing missing shingles is vital for maintaining your roof’s integrity.

8. Finding Granules in the Gutters

Asphalt shingles often lose granules over time. If you see a lot of granules in your gutters, it’s a sign that your shingles are breaking down and may need to be replaced.

9. Moss or Algae Growth

If you see moss or algae on your roof, it’s probably retaining too much water. Too much moisture can lead to shingle decay, which is when you would need a new roof.

10. Neighbors Are Replacing Their Roofs

If several of your neighbors are installing new roofs, it might be a sign that yours needs replacing, too. Homes in the same neighborhood experience similar weather conditions, so your roof may also be damaged. Consider this a proactive warning to assess the state of your own roof.

11. Missing Gutter Guards, Flashing, or Fascia

If several of your neighbors are installing new roofs, it might be a sign that yours needs replacing, too. Homes in the same neighborhood experience similar weather conditions, so your roof may also be damaged. Consider this a proactive warning to assess the state of your own roof.

12. High Energy Bills

When your roof gets old, it loses its insulating properties and starts letting the cold and heat into your home. As a result, you might notice that your energy bills are increasing as you turn up the thermostat to keep up with the temperature fluctuations.

What to Do if You Need to Replace Your Roof

Identifying one or more of these warning signs is how to know when to replace your roof. Contact a professional roofing contractor like M&M Gutters to assess the damage and discuss your options for roof replacement.

How Often Should a Roof Be Replaced?

You should replace your roof every 20 to 30 years, regardless of your local climate. In snowy areas like Logan, roofs may wear out faster due to the heavy snowfall. In St. George, UV exposure can affect the quality of your home. Regular roof inspections can help you determine when a replacement is needed.

What Is the Average Age of a Roof Before Replacement?

The average lifespan of a roof is 20 to 30 years, but this timeline can vary depending on several factors, including weather patterns, material type, and the level of roof care.

Keep Your Home Safe With a Solid Roof

Protecting your home starts with a sturdy roof. By recognizing the signs you need a new roof, you can address issues proactively and prevent further damage to your home.

Still not sure how to tell if you need a new roof? We can help! Contact us today to speak with a professional about the best steps for your home.

h1: 3 Common Reasons Why Your Gutter System Is Leaking
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
If your gutter system on your home is leaking, it cannot perform and do the job they are meant to do.

A leaky gutter system can be very stressful for homeowners. When your gutters are leaking, they can no longer effectively nor efficiently direct rainwater away from your house. This can lead to a myriad of issues, including water damage to the interior and exterior of your home, erosion, and foundational issues. Thankfully, knowing what to look for and understanding the common causes and reasons for leaky gutters can significantly reduce the chances of leaks and other issues.

Continue reading to learn more about the common reasons gutters leak.

Why Is My Gutter System Leaking?

  1. Older Gutters — While leaks can occur on new gutters, you’re more likely to find leaks in an aging system. This is likely because the gutter sections are sealed to each other or screwed to one another. With each passing storm, the sealant deteriorates, and the screws are loosened or fall out. Thankfully, in many cases, you can close up holes and other leaks with a silicone waterproof sealant, extending the life of your gutters.
  2. Clogged Gutters — One of the most common causes of leaky gutters (and, luckily, one of the easiest to fix!) is clogged gutters. Homeowners that avoid and postpone the seemingly daunting and tedious task of cleaning out their gutter system often find themselves dealing with leaks. Clogged gutters lead to overflows and leaks that can run down the sides of your house and lead to significant damage.
  3. Damaged Gutters — Season after season, your gutters endure plenty of wear and tear, which inevitably lead to leaks, holes, and other damage. Plenty of the damage that occurs can be fixed yourself. However, larger holes, breaks, and more significant damage should be handled by a professional that knows what they’re doing.

How to Avoid a Leaky Gutter System

Thankfully, avoiding a leaky gutter system is relatively easy — all it takes is a little time and dedication:

  • Clean your gutters whenever necessary and, at the very least, twice each year
  • Inspect for damage after every major storm
  • Check for loose sections and screws
  • Make necessary repairs sooner rather than later
  • Invest in leaf guards and ice and snow melt systems

title: 3 Ways To Extend the Life of Your Home’s Siding
meta: Learn key strategies to prolong the durability and appearance of your home siding effectively.
h1: 3 Ways to Extend the Life of Your Home’s Siding
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Extend the life of your home’s siding by implementing a few tips from our team of knowledgeable professionals.

The exterior of your home holds many responsibilities, and keeping it in good condition allows it to do its job. Siding is designed to last for a long time, but it cannot work how it is meant to without proper care and maintenance.

Constant exposure to extreme elements can significantly impact its lifespan and function effectively. By implementing a few pro tips, you can keep your siding in tip-top shape for decades to come.

Keep reading to learn more.

3 Ways You Can Extend the Life of Your Home’s Siding

These simple yet effective tips will help improve your home’s siding look and function. Here’s what to do:

  1. Examine It Regularly — Taking a walk around the perimeter of your house to inspect your siding is a great way to ensure it is still in good shape. Keep your eyes open for damaged areas, such as dents, chips, or holes. Intense winds can cause your siding to loosen, raise, or otherwise become damaged.
    There isn’t a right answer as to how often you should examine your exteriors, but once every season and after intense storms should be sufficient. When you come across any damage, have it repaired as soon as possible to avoid further damage.
  2. Clean It Often — It’s no secret that the siding wrapping your home takes regular beatings; between the elements, critters, and people, the exteriors of your home can begin to look rough. Keep your siding looking great by eliminating grime, mold, and dirt with regular washes. Use your hose and a mixture of water and white vinegar to scrub away any imperfections.
    Keep in mind that using a power washer can damage the siding if not used properly. In some cases, using a power washer can also void the manufacturer’s warranty.
  3. Treat It Carefully — Siding was built to last, but that doesn’t make it indestructible. If you want to increase the life of your siding, it is crucial to treat it carefully. This means avoiding using barbecue grills, fire pits, and compact radiators nearby.
    It also means abstaining from hitting it with anything, including your lawnmower, edger, or a ball. By making conscious consideration and effort to treat your siding carefully, you can add years to the life of your exteriors.

h1: 5 Reasons To Fix Your Damaged Siding Right Away
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Repairing damaged siding as soon as possible can help you to avoid other potentially serious home issues.

One of the best things about siding, and likely the top reason homeowners opt for the material, is the little maintenance it requires. Unfortunately, however, when it becomes damaged, you should address it right away. Because putting off repairs can lead to serious problems down the line, promptly taking action is essential.

Find out why you should fix your broken siding as soon as possible below.

5 Reasons to Fix Your Damaged Siding Right Away

If you want to keep your home’s exterior in good shape, proper care and maintenance are crucial. This includes repairing your siding when it becomes damaged. Here are several benefits that come with fixing your broken siding right away:

  1. Quick Action Prevents Further Damage — If you put off repairing your siding, you are leaving your home susceptible to more damage, such as insect and other critter infestations and water damage. Of the two, water damage is more serious. It has the potential of causing rot which can lead to other problems, like sagging ceilings and peeling paint, and other issues that can also negatively impact your health, like mold and mildew growth. Water damage can also increase indoor humidity and fog up your windows. Thankfully, by quickly repairing broken siding, you can avoid these issues!
  2. Save Money — As the problems with your damaged siding become bigger, the more expensive it is to repair. The damage can become so severe that replacing an entire wall, window, or beam is necessary. In the long run, it’s a lot easier on your wallet to fix the damaged area before it grows.
  3. Quick and Relatively Easy Fix — Fixing broken siding is quick and relatively easy. In addition to saving you money, fast action takes far less time to fix than large, more serious issues. We’re talking hours as opposed to days.
  4. Keep Up the Curb Appeal — Broken siding is undoubtedly rough on the eyes! If keeping your home looking good is important to you, or you are planning to sell your house in the near future, repairing damaged areas on the exterior of your property is essential!
  5. Improve the Energy Efficiency of Your House — Siding plays an important role in the thermal envelope of your home, just like your roof, doors, and windows. An energy-efficient house will have a thermal envelope that effectively and successfully minimizes heat gain during warmer months and heat loss during the colder months. Broken siding introduces leaks that only compromise your home’s thermal envelope and lessen energy efficiency, increasing your energy consumption (also read: your bills!).

title: 5 Signs It’s Time To Replace Your Siding | M&M Gutters

h1: 5 Signs It’s Time to Replace Your Siding
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
If you want to protect your damaged exteriors against the elements and improve your home’s appearance, you may need to replace your siding.

Most people go right to the roof as the front defense in protecting your home and everything inside from the harsh elements. However, many other components are just as important as your roof, such as your property’s siding. In most cases, the siding will need to be repaired and, later, replaced entirely. You can learn more about the signs you need to replace your siding below.

Continue reading to learn more.

5 Signs You Should Replace Your Siding

The siding on your house has several different responsibilities; at the top of those is protecting your home and aesthetics. When your siding is run down and damaged, it cannot do those things effectively. Here are five signs it is time to replace your siding:

  1. Blistering and Bubbling — You’ve probably seen homes that were built 40 to 60 years ago that have blistering or bubbling siding. This has turned many people off to the idea of wrapping their homes in the material. But it’s important to remember that the siding used in previous decades is not the same as its modern counterpart.

Today’s siding is more durable, stronger, and resistant to extreme temperatures and weather. Moreover, with proper care and maintenance, today’s materials and manufacturing techniques can look new for decades.

  1. Cracks, Chips, and Dents — In extreme cases, storms can lead to siding damage. Strong windows can hurl hail and debris into your home, causing dents, cracks, and chips. Thankfully, a few dents here and there typically won’t cause significant moisture damage, but cracks and chips can expose the underlying structure of your home to water, which could lead to further issues.
  2. High Utility Bills — You may not have realized that your high energy bills could be associated with your siding, but it’s true! Older siding is not nearly as energy-efficient as today’s options. You’ll notice a difference in how much you’re paying in bills after your old siding is removed and the new siding professionally installed.
  3. Rippling and Warping — Poorly installed siding or long periods can lead to rippling and warping siding. In addition to being unattractive, it can also allow water to get in where it shouldn’t. New siding should be installed to avoid water damage issues and restore your curb appeal.
  4. Animal Damage — If your home is near any mountains or wooden area, it’s more than likely that your house has become a home to more than just you and your family. Birds, mice, squirrels, and other small critters seek warmth in colder months. If your siding is old, you may want to consider replacing it to protect your property from animal damage.

If it’s time to replace your siding on your property, contact the experts at M & M Gutters & Exteriors. With decades of industry experience, no job is too big or small for our professional team. Our skilled technicians are fully licensed and insured. We are committed to delivering high-quality service, gutters, and siding to homes and businesses in Salt Lake, Davis, Weber, Utah, and Summit counties in Utah. Contact us today to learn more.

title: 5 Signs Your Home Needs a New Gutter System | M&M Gutters
meta: Spot these five signs to determine when it's time for a gutter system overhaul with M&M Gutters.
h1: 5 Signs Your Home Needs a New Gutter System
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
If your gutters are leaky, sagging, or cracked, it could be time for a new gutter system. Keep reading to find out why new gutters are so vital.

Gutters play an essential role in keeping your home functioning at its best. They are responsible for directing water away from the exterior walls of your home, doors, windows, and foundation, preventing water from getting inside your house. It’s essential to take care of your gutters and clean them periodically to ensure they last as long as possible. Even with regular care and maintenance, you will need to repair or replace your gutters at some point to make sure your home stays protected.

Here are the five signs you should look for that indicate that you need to replace your gutters.

Your Home Needs a New Gutter System if You Notice

To help determine when your home needs new gutters, keep your eye out for the following warning signs:

  1. Sagging Gutters — One of the easiest ways to tell your house gutters need some TLC is when your gutter system begins to sag or pull away from your roofline. Gutters that are in well-working order should never pull away or sag from your house. Sagging and pulling can signify that your gutters are full of water and are drooping due to the weight. This could require basic repairs or, if significant damage has occurred, your house may need a whole new system.
  2. Cracks and Leaks — Cracks and leaks in your gutters are obviously a concern — even small cracks and leaks can lead to big problems. The tiniest crack can quickly turn into a large crack and cause significant damage to your home fascia boards, foundation, and your home’s exterior materials.
  3. Pooling Water at the Base of Your Home — The main job of a gutter system is to direct water away from your property’s foundation. Pooling water at your home’s foundation can lead to serious, costly issues. If you noticed water pooling near your foundation, this could indicate that your gutter system is not working correctly. This problem could be caused by something as simple as a clog or a defect in the entire gutter system. Either way, it’s crucial to address it right away.
  4. Peeling Paint and Orange Flecks — Painted gutters are built to withstand the seasons’ elements and general wear and tear. However, once gutters become old, you’ll find that the paint on your gutters begins to peel off, and bits of orange flecks appear from the beginning stages of rust thanks to a constant presence of water. This typically means water is not moving through your gutters as it should, indicating that it might be time for a new gutter system.
  5. Water Damage and Water Marks — On a sunny, at least once a year, check for water damage and watermarks just below your gutters. Finding either of these could indicate that your gutter system is leaking or overflowing, which can cause expensive damage to the exterior of your home.

Need a New Gutter System? Contact M & M Gutters & Exteriors

If your Northern Utah home needs a new gutter system or requires repairs, contact the pros at M & M Gutters & Exteriors. With over 25 years in the industry, our knowledgeable professionals specialize in commercial buildings, homes, apartment buildings, and more. Old or new, we can get it done! Contact our fully licensed and insured team today!

title: 90 Pound Felt: Underlayment or Standalone? A Complete Breakdown - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Discover 90 pound roofing felt: specs, installation, pros/cons vs. modified bitumen. Ideal for low-slope roofs—standalone or underlayment?
h1: 90 Pound Felt: Underlayment or Standalone? A Complete Breakdown
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
What You Need to Know About 90 Pound Roofing Felt

90 pound roofing felt is a heavy-duty, mineral-surfaced roll roofing product designed primarily for low-slope roofs. It is not the same as standard felt underlayment — it functions as a standalone roof surface.

Quick answers:

  • What it is: A roll roofing membrane made from a fiberglass or organic mat, coated with asphalt, and topped with ceramic mineral granules
  • What it’s used for: Low-slope roofs on sheds, porches, utility buildings, and similar structures
  • How long it lasts: Roughly 8 to 10 years when properly sealed; often closer to 5 years on very low slopes
  • Can it replace underlayment? No — it is a surface covering, not an underlayment
  • Typical roll size: Approximately 36 inches wide by 36 feet long, covering 1 square (108 sq ft)
  • Typical cost: Around $150–$160 per roll for quality products

Despite the name, 90 pound roofing felt is not felt paper like #15 or #30. It is heavier, thicker, and built to be the final exposed layer on a roof — not a layer hidden beneath shingles.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors, and after 30+ years helping Utah homeowners with roofing projects, I’ve seen how often 90 pound roofing felt is misunderstood — and misinstalled. Let’s break down exactly what it is, where it works, and where it falls short.

Simple 90 pound roofing felt word guide:

  • ASTM D226 Type 1 and Type 2
  • What is ASTM D226

What is 90 Pound Roofing Felt?

To understand 90 pound roofing felt, we first have to clear up a major naming confusion. In the roofing world, “felt” usually refers to the thin, black paper you put under shingles. However, #90 (as it’s often called) is actually mineral-surfaced roll roofing.

Its composition is much more robust than standard underlayment. It typically features a strong fiberglass mat—though some older versions used an organic mat—that is saturated and coated on both sides with weathering-grade asphalt. To provide protection against the sun and foot traffic, the top surface is embedded with ceramic mineral granules, much like the surface of a standard asphalt shingle.

Because of this heavy coating and granule layer, it is significantly thicker than underlayment. If you are wondering how thick is roofing felt, standard #15 felt is paper-thin, while 90 pound roofing felt can be upwards of 50 to 90 mils thick. It is designed to be the “roof” itself, not just a backup layer.

For a deeper dive into the basics of the “felt” family, you can check out our more info about what roofing felt is guide. In terms of industry standards, while standard underlayments often fall under ASTM D226 or ASTM D4869, #90 roll roofing is built to handle direct exposure to the elements, including snow and UV rays common here in Northern Utah.

Distinguishing #90 from #15 and #30 Felts

The numbers #15, #30, and #90 used to refer to the actual weight of the material per 100 square feet (one “square”). In the old days, 15-pound felt weighed 15 pounds per square. Modern manufacturing has made materials lighter but stronger, so today’s “15-pound” felt might only weigh 8 to 12 pounds.

However, 90 pound roofing felt has stayed true to its heavy-duty roots. It is drastically heavier and tougher than its counterparts.

Feature#15 Felt#30 Felt#90 Roll Roofing
Primary UseUnderlayment (Steep Slope)Underlayment (Heavy Duty)Standalone Roof Surface
Weight per Roll~30 lbs~45 lbs~78-90 lbs
Coverage400 sq. ft.200 sq. ft.100 sq. ft.
SurfaceSmooth AsphaltSmooth AsphaltMineral Granules
DurabilityLow (Tears easily)MediumHigh (Tear resistant)

When you are choosing between Type 1 and Type 2 felt, you are usually looking for a layer to go under shingles. If you are looking at a low-slope porch or a shed where you don’t want to install individual shingles, #90 is your candidate.

Key Specifications of 90 Pound Roofing Felt

If you’re planning a DIY project or checking a contractor’s quote in Salt Lake County, you need to know the “specs.” While it’s called “90 pound,” a modern roll of G.A.P. or Tarco mineral-surfaced roofing actually weighs about 78 to 80 lbs per roll.

Here are the typical measurements:

  • Dimensions: 36 inches wide by 36 feet long (some rolls are 39 3/8″ wide).
  • Coverage: 108 square feet. After accounting for the necessary laps (overlaps), one roll covers exactly 1 square (100 square feet) of roof area.
  • Thickness: Approximately 50 to 90 mils.
  • Packaging: Usually 25 rolls per pallet.

One of the perks of 90 pound roofing felt is the aesthetic variety. Because it uses ceramic slate granules, it comes in several colors to match your main house shingles. Common options include:

  • Black/Charcoal: The most popular for a sleek look.
  • White: Great for reflecting heat (though it shows dirt faster).
  • Brown: Often used for sheds and rustic structures.
  • Green: A classic choice for utility buildings and cabins.

Primary Uses and Suitable Applications

In our 30+ years at M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we typically see 90 pound roofing felt used on “low-slope” applications. A low-slope roof is generally defined as having a pitch between 2:12 and 4:12. If your roof is flatter than 2:12, you really should be looking at more robust commercial-grade options like EPDM or TPO.

Common applications include:

  1. Sheds and Barns: It’s the most economical way to get a finished roof on a utility building.
  2. Screened Porches: Since porches often have a lower pitch than the main house, #90 is a frequent choice.
  3. Carports: It provides a quick, water-shedding surface that matches the home.
  4. Secondary Water Barrier: Sometimes used in very specific valley constructions or as a heavy-duty liner.

It’s important to understand the weights and measures of underlayment for roofing to ensure you aren’t overloading your structure. Because #90 is heavy, the roof deck needs to be solid and in good condition.

While it is widely used across the country and even meets strict standards like the Florida Building Code, here in Utah, we have to consider snow load. If you use #90 on a low-slope roof in Summit County or Weber County, you must ensure the seams are perfectly sealed to prevent ice damming from forcing water under the laps. You can learn more about how different materials handle these slopes in our guide on understanding roofing materials and types.

Installation and Performance of 90 Pound Roofing Felt

Installation is where most people go wrong. Because 90 pound roofing felt is stiff and heavy, it doesn’t “self-heal” or seal as easily as a standard shingle might in the sun.

There are three main ways to install it:

  • Cold Adhesive: This is the most common DIY and residential method. A “lap cement” or specialized asphalt adhesive is spread on the deck and at the seams.
  • Hot Mopping: This is a professional method involving molten asphalt. It creates an incredibly strong bond but requires specialized equipment and carries higher safety risks.
  • Nailing (with Sealed Laps): Nails are used to hold the sheet in place, but the laps must be sealed with adhesive to prevent wind-driven rain from getting underneath.

When installing, always refer to a comprehensive look at roofing felt standards to ensure your project meets local building codes.

Proper Installation of 90 Pound Roofing Felt

To get that 8 to 10-year lifespan, you can’t cut corners. Here is the professional way to do it:

  1. Preparation: Start with a clean, dry, and smooth deck. Any protruding nails will eventually poke through the felt.
  2. Drip Edge: Install a T-drip edge at the eaves.
  3. The “Starter” Strip: Some pros use a 9-inch wide starter strip of the felt itself.
  4. Lapping: Apply the rolls in a “shingle fashion,” starting from the bottom and working up. Each layer should overlap the one below it by at least 2 to 4 inches. For very low slopes, a 19-inch overlap (double coverage) is often recommended.
  5. Sealing: Use a generous amount of lap cement at every seam. If you see “wrinkles” or “fishmouths,” the material wasn’t rolled out flat or the adhesive wasn’t applied evenly. These wrinkles are the #1 cause of premature leaks.
  6. Edge Work: Use gravel guards or snipped and folded drip edges at the corners to ensure water is directed away from the fascia.

Common DIY Mistake: Many people try to “nail only.” Without adhesive at the seams, wind will eventually lift the edges, and capillary action will pull water right under the felt and into your plywood.

90 Pound Roofing Felt vs. Modified Bitumen

We often get asked: “Is this #90 felt or Modified Bitumen (Mod Bit)?” They look very similar because they both come in granulated rolls. However, they are very different beasts.

The Tear Test: The easiest way to tell them apart is to try and tear a small piece. 90 pound roofing felt is made with a fiberglass or organic mat; it is relatively brittle and will tear if you pull hard enough. Modified Bitumen is “modified” with rubber (SBS) or plastic (APP) polymers. It is extremely stretchy and almost impossible to tear by hand.

Comparison at a Glance:

  • Underside: Mod Bit usually has a glossy black, smooth underside (especially the torch-down or peel-and-stick versions). #90 felt usually has a duller, asphalt-saturated finish.
  • Durability: Mod Bit can last 15–20 years. #90 felt typically lasts 5–10 years.
  • Installation: Mod Bit often requires a torch or is self-adhered. #90 felt is usually “mopped” or glued.
  • Price: 90 pound roofing felt is significantly cheaper, making it the “budget” choice for utility structures.

Pros, Cons, and Limitations

Using 90 Pound Roofing Felt as a Standalone Surface

Is it right for your project? Let’s weigh the options.

The Pros:

  • Cost-Effective: It is one of the cheapest ways to cover a low-slope roof.
  • DIY Friendly: Unlike torch-down roofing (which can literally burn your house down if you aren’t careful), #90 felt can be installed with basic tools and cold adhesive.
  • Availability: You can find it at almost any hardware store in Salt Lake City or Davis County.
  • Breathability: Organic-based felts allow some moisture to escape the building, reducing the risk of rot in certain conditions.

The Cons:

  • Short Lifespan: In the harsh Utah sun and snow, don’t expect more than 10 years. On flat roofs with ponding water, it might only last 5.
  • Maintenance: You need to check the seams every year. If the adhesive dries out and cracks, leaks follow immediately.
  • Fragility: It becomes brittle in the winter. If you walk on it when it’s freezing, you can crack the membrane.
  • UV Sensitivity: Once the granules start to rub off (granule loss), the asphalt underneath degrades rapidly under UV light.

Frequently Asked Questions about 90lb Felt

Is 90-pound roofing felt the same as underlayment?

No. While it has the word “felt” in the name, it is a roll roofing membrane. Standard underlayment (like #15 or #30) is meant to be covered by shingles. 90-pound felt is meant to be the final, exposed layer of the roof. Using it as an underlayment is generally a waste of money and can create a surface that is too “slick” for shingles to bond to properly.

Can you install 90-pound felt over an existing roof?

While some people do it, we don’t recommend it. Installing new #90 over an old, wrinkled roof will result in a “telegraphed” finish—meaning the new roof will be just as lumpy as the old one. This creates water pockets and speeds up failure. It’s always better to tear off the old material to inspect the wood deck for rot.

How do you identify 90-pound felt on an existing structure?

Look at the seams and the texture. If it’s a 3-foot wide roll with mineral granules and it feels somewhat “papery” or brittle when you pick at an edge, it’s likely 90 pound roofing felt. If it feels rubbery and thick, you’re likely looking at Modified Bitumen.

Conclusion

90 pound roofing felt is a reliable, budget-friendly solution for low-slope utility buildings, sheds, and porches. It provides a finished look that matches your shingles without the complexity of a commercial roofing system. However, its performance depends entirely on the quality of the installation—specifically how well those seams are sealed.

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we’ve spent over 30 years serving Salt Lake City and the surrounding counties. We know that a roof is only as good as its weakest point. Whether you’re looking for a quick shed roof or a full residential replacement, we bring the expertise and 3D visualization tools to ensure the job is done right the first time.

Don’t leave your low-slope roof to chance. If you’re in Northern Utah and need a professional eye on your next project, reach out to us today.

title: Arc de Triomphe: Measuring Your Arch Window for Replacement - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Learn how to measure arch window for replacement with step-by-step instructions, tools, and tips for perfect arched window sizing.
h1: Arc de Triomphe: Measuring Your Arch Window for Replacement
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
Why Getting Your Arch Window Measurements Right Matters

Knowing how to measure arch window for replacement correctly is the difference between a window that fits perfectly and one that costs you time, money, and headaches.

Here’s a quick answer to get you started:

How to measure an arch window for replacement:

  1. Measure the base width — from the left to the right corner inside the window opening
  2. Measure the center height — from the bottom up to the tallest point at the center
  3. Check for a perfect arch — height should equal exactly half the base width
  4. Measure the jamb depth — you need at least 3¼ inches for replacement
  5. Check for square — measure both diagonals; if they differ by more than ½ inch, your frame is out of square
  6. Round to the nearest ⅛ inch — always record width × height

Arched windows add a classic, timeless look to any home. They bring in natural light and give your exterior real curb appeal. But their curved shape makes measuring trickier than a standard rectangular window — and a wrong measurement means a wrong order.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors, and after more than 30 years serving Utah homeowners on exterior projects — including window replacements — I know how a precise approach to how to measure arch window for replacement saves costly mistakes before they happen. Let’s walk through everything you need to do it right.

Common how to measure arch window for replacement vocab:

  • how do you measure a replacement window
  • how to measure for replacement windows in a brick home
  • how to measure house windows for replacement

Essential Tools and Safety for Arched Window Measurement

Before we start measuring, let’s get the right tools together. Arched windows are not the place for “close enough,” and cloth measuring tapes belong in the sewing room, not on a replacement window project.

You’ll need:

  • Steel tape measure
  • Pencil
  • Notepad or printed measuring worksheet
  • Painter’s tape
  • Level
  • Straightedge or framing square
  • Step ladder, if needed
  • Camera or phone for reference photos
  • Butcher paper or kraft paper for templates
  • Utility knife or scissors for template testing
  • Helper, especially for wide or high windows

A steel tape measure matters because it stays straight and gives more consistent readings. A floppy tape can sag across a wide arch and quietly add an expensive mistake to your order.

For specialty windows, it also helps to review general guidance on measuring skylights and arched windows, especially if your project includes a skylight or another hard-to-reach opening.

Now let’s talk safety, because no window is worth a trip to urgent care.

If the window is high on a wall:

  • Use a stable ladder on level ground.
  • Keep three points of contact on the ladder.
  • Do not stand on the top step.
  • Have someone hold the ladder.
  • Never lean far to one side to “just reach it.”
  • Move the ladder instead of stretching.

If measuring requires roof access, we strongly recommend calling a professional. Roof pitch, loose granules, ice, wind, and Utah’s freeze-thaw conditions can turn a simple measurement into a dangerous situation. If roof access is unavoidable, use proper fall protection and never work alone.

Also, take pictures as you measure. A photo showing the tape measure in place can help you or your installer verify the number later. Future-you will be grateful. Future-you may even buy present-you a cookie.

How to Measure Arch Window for Replacement: Step-by-Step

This is the core process for how to measure arch window for replacement. We’ll keep it simple, but do not rush. Measure each window individually, even if two arches look identical. Homes settle, frames shift, and “identical” windows often have tiny differences.

For more general window sizing help, we also recommend our guide: Measuring Up: How to Get Perfect Window Dimensions Every Time.

1. Measure the base width

Measure the inside width at the bottom of the arch opening.

Place your tape at the lower left corner where the arch begins and measure straight across to the lower right corner. This is the base of the arch.

Record it as:

  • Base width: ____ inches

For replacement windows, measure the opening itself, not the decorative trim or casing. Trim can hide the real frame dimensions, and ordering from trim-to-trim measurements can create a bad fit.

2. Measure the center height

Find the center point of the base width. The easiest way is to divide the width by two and mark the center lightly with painter’s tape.

From that center point, measure straight up to the tallest point of the arch.

Record it as:

  • Center height: ____ inches

This measurement tells you the rise of the arch. On a perfect half-round arch, this number should be exactly half of the base width.

Example:

Base WidthPerfect Arch Height
48 inches24 inches
60 inches30 inches
72 inches36 inches

If your 60-inch-wide arch measures 30 inches high, you have a perfect arch. If it measures 26 inches, 34 inches, or anything else, it is not a perfect arch.

3. Measure the total height if the arch sits above a rectangular section

Some arched windows are a true half-circle sitting directly on the sill. Others are elongated arches, with vertical sides below the curve.

If your arch has straight vertical legs, measure:

  • Full height from sill to highest point
  • Leg height from sill to where the curve begins
  • Arch rise from where the curve begins to the highest point

Record all three. We’ll cover elongated arches in more detail below.

4. Measure the jamb depth

Jamb depth is the distance from the interior face of the window opening to the exterior side of the frame area, or from the front of the opening back to the trim or obstruction that limits the replacement unit.

For many replacement windows, you need at least 3 1/4 inches of opening depth. If you do not have enough depth, the project may require a different product, trim modification, or full-frame replacement approach.

Record:

  • Jamb depth, left: ____ inches
  • Jamb depth, center: ____ inches
  • Jamb depth, right: ____ inches

Use the smallest measurement if the depth varies.

5. Measure diagonals to check square

Even though the top is curved, the lower opening and frame still need to be checked for distortion.

Measure from the lower left corner to the upper right transition point, then from the lower right corner to the upper left transition point. If you are measuring a full arched unit with a rectangular section below, measure the diagonals across the rectangular portion.

If the diagonal measurements differ by more than 1/2 inch, the opening is considered significantly out of square. That does not automatically mean replacement is impossible, but it does mean you should not order based on one quick width and height measurement.

6. Record measurements in width x height format

Window measurements are normally written as width x height.

For example:

  • 60 inches x 30 inches
  • 48 1/8 inches x 24 1/16 inches
  • 72 inches x 36 inches

Keep your notes clean and labeled by room. “Big arch upstairs” may make sense today. In two weeks, when you’re comparing three similar windows, it will feel like a riddle from a wizard.

7. Round carefully

Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch unless the manufacturer or installer asks for another precision.

For replacement windows, do not automatically round up. A window that is too large will not fit. In many replacement situations, we measure in multiple places and use the smallest dimension as the controlling number, then let the manufacturer or installer determine proper clearance.

For some window treatments, the rounding rule may be different. For example, certain inside-mounted skylight shades may require rounding up to the nearest 1/8 inch and at least 2 inches of mounting depth. That is why it is important to separate “replacement window measurements” from “shade or blind measurements.”

Perfect Arches vs. Non-Perfect Arches and Specialty Shapes

A perfect arch is a half-circle. The height of the arch equals exactly half the base width.

Formula:

Perfect arch height = base width ÷ 2

So if the base width is 64 inches, the perfect arch height is 32 inches.

A non-perfect arch does not follow that ratio. It may be flatter, taller, stretched, eyebrow-shaped, elongated, or asymmetrical. Non-perfect arches are common in custom homes and older homes throughout Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County, Utah County, Summit County, Tooele County, Davis County, Weber County, and Northern Utah.

This is where careful measuring matters. It is also where a paper template can save the day.

For other curved-window measuring concepts, see our related guide on bay and bow replacement measurements.

Arch TypeWhat It Looks LikeMeasurements NeededSpecial Notes
Perfect archHalf-circleBase width, center height, jamb depthHeight equals half the width
Non-perfect archCurve is flatter or taller than half-circleBase width, center height, multiple curve points, templateDo not assume standard sizing
Elongated archStraight sides with arch on topBase width, full height, leg heights, arch riseMeasure both legs separately
Quarter archOne straight side and one curved sideBase width, straight-side height, tallest point, templateOften needs extra verification
Eyebrow archLow, shallow curveWidth, rise, multiple points along curveTemplate is strongly recommended

How to measure arch window for replacement when dealing with elongated shapes

An elongated arch has vertical sides below the curved top. Think of it like a rectangle wearing a fancy hat.

To measure an elongated arch:

  1. Measure the base width at the bottom opening.
  2. Measure the full height from sill to highest point.
  3. Measure the left leg height from sill to where the curve begins.
  4. Measure the right leg height from sill to where the curve begins.
  5. Measure the arch rise from the curve-start line to the highest point.
  6. Measure jamb depth.
  7. Check diagonals across the rectangular lower section.

Record:

  • Base width: ____ inches
  • Full height: ____ inches
  • Left leg height: ____ inches
  • Right leg height: ____ inches
  • Arch rise: ____ inches
  • Jamb depth: ____ inches

Do not assume the left and right legs are the same height. If one side is even 1/4 inch different, the arch may not sit correctly without adjustment.

For elongated arches, a template is often helpful because the curve may not be a standard radius.

How to measure arch window for replacement with quarter-circle designs

A quarter arch is usually one-fourth of a circle. It may appear above a door, beside another window, or as part of a larger architectural design.

To measure a quarter arch:

  1. Measure the base width along the bottom.
  2. Measure the straight vertical side from bottom to tallest point.
  3. Measure the curved side height at several points if possible.
  4. Measure the jamb depth.
  5. Note which direction the curve faces: left-hand or right-hand.
  6. Create a paper template if the shape is custom or uneven.

Quarter arches are easy to flip by mistake when ordering. Always label:

  • Top
  • Bottom
  • Room side
  • Exterior side
  • Left curve or right curve

If the window is part of a pair, label each unit separately. “Left arch” should mean left as viewed from inside the room unless your order form says otherwise.

Inside Mount vs. Outside Mount and Depth Requirements

Inside mount and outside mount language is most common with window treatments, but the idea also helps homeowners understand how a replacement unit interacts with the opening.

An inside-mounted product fits within the existing opening. An outside-mounted product overlaps or attaches outside the opening. For actual replacement windows, this often translates into insert replacement versus full-frame or custom installation planning.

Use an inside-style replacement approach when:

  • The existing frame is sound.
  • The opening is reasonably square.
  • The jamb depth is sufficient.
  • There is no major water damage.
  • You want to preserve existing interior trim.

Use an outside-style or full-frame approach when:

  • The frame is out of square by more than 1/2 inch.
  • There is rot, water damage, or structural movement.
  • The opening is too shallow.
  • The existing frame is failing.
  • You need better flashing, insulation, or exterior integration.

For deeper replacement planning, see Measure Twice, Order Once: Your Guide to Perfect Replacement Window Sizing and this professional overview of how to assess windows for replacement.

Depth requirements to keep in mind:

Product or Installation TypeCommon Minimum Depth
Replacement arched window opening3 1/4 inches
Inside-mounted arched treatment1 1/2 inches minimum
Fully recessed inside-mounted treatmentAround 2 1/4 inches
Some skylight window treatments1 1/2 to 2 inches

Always verify the exact product specifications before ordering. As of June 2026, many custom products have their own sizing rules, and specialty arches may have maximum size limits. Some arched window treatments, for example, may top out around 73 1/2 inches wide by 36 5/8 inches high. Replacement window limits vary by product line, glass type, and structural needs.

How to check for inside mount suitability

Use this checklist:

  • Is the opening deep enough?
  • Is the frame square enough?
  • Is the sill level?
  • Are the side jambs plumb?
  • Is the existing frame free of rot?
  • Is there enough flat mounting surface?
  • Will the new unit interfere with trim, tile, blinds, or shutters?

If the answer is “no” to any of these, pause before ordering. The opening may still be workable, but it may need professional evaluation.

Utah homes also deal with sun exposure, snow, wind, and freeze-thaw cycles. In Northern Utah, proper flashing and sealing around specialty windows is just as important as the glass size. A beautifully measured window that is poorly sealed is still a problem waiting for the next storm.

Creating a Physical Template and Verifying Your Dimensions

For perfect arches, numbers may be enough. For non-perfect arches, elongated arches, eyebrow arches, quarter arches, or older custom openings, a physical template is often the best way to avoid guesswork.

A template is especially useful when:

  • The arch is not a perfect half-circle.
  • The curve is uneven.
  • The window is old or custom-built.
  • The opening is out of square.
  • You are ordering specialty glass or a custom unit.
  • The manufacturer requests a template.
  • The arch shape is hard to describe with simple width and height.

To create a paper template:

  1. Tape butcher paper or kraft paper over the inside of the window opening.
  2. Keep the paper smooth and tight.
  3. Trace the inside frame edge carefully.
  4. Mark the base line.
  5. Mark the highest point.
  6. Write the exact measurements directly on the paper.
  7. Label “Top.”
  8. Label “Room Side.”
  9. Label the room name.
  10. Add your name and date.
  11. Cut out the template and place it back in the opening to test the fit.
  12. Roll the template instead of folding it.

Do not fold the template. Folds can distort the curve. Roll it like a poster.

This process is similar to the careful approach used when replacing glass, where shape, edge conditions, and exact dimensions matter. For more on glass-specific measuring, read Crystal Clear Measurements: Your Guide to Replacing Window Glass.

How to verify your measurements before ordering

Before you place an order, go through this final check:

  • Re-measure the base width.
  • Re-measure the center height.
  • Re-measure jamb depth.
  • Confirm whether the arch is perfect or non-perfect.
  • Check both diagonals.
  • Confirm inside vs outside or insert vs full-frame approach.
  • Compare your numbers to your template.
  • Review manufacturer sizing instructions.
  • Take photos of the tape measure in place.
  • Have another person read the measurements back to you.
  • Confirm all notes use width x height format.

Here is a simple measurement worksheet:

MeasurementFirst ReadingSecond ReadingFinal Number
Base width
Center height
Full height, if elongated
Left leg height
Right leg height
Jamb depth
Diagonal 1
Diagonal 2

If two readings do not match, measure a third time. The tape measure does not get a vote; the correct number wins.

Frequently Asked Questions about Arched Window Sizing

Arched windows create a few recurring questions, especially when homeowners are trying to order replacements without turning their living room into a geometry classroom. Here are the answers we give most often.

What is the mathematical ratio of a perfect arch window?

A perfect arch has a height that equals exactly half of its base width.

Formula:

Height = Width ÷ 2

Example:

  • 50-inch width = 25-inch arch height
  • 64-inch width = 32-inch arch height
  • 72-inch width = 36-inch arch height

If the height is not half the width, the window is not a perfect arch. That does not mean anything is wrong with it. It simply means it is a specialty shape and needs more careful measuring.

Should I round my arched window measurements up or down?

For replacement windows, measure to the nearest 1/8 inch and record the exact numbers. Do not make your own deductions unless the manufacturer or installer specifically tells you to.

General rule:

  • Measure width in more than one place.
  • Measure height in more than one place.
  • Use the smallest dimension when evaluating fit.
  • Record to the nearest 1/8 inch.
  • Let the window professional or manufacturer determine production deductions.

For inside-mounted window treatments, some products require rounding down to the nearest 1/8 inch, while others, such as certain skylight shades, may require rounding up to the nearest 1/8 inch. Product instructions control the final rounding rule.

When in doubt, record the raw measurement exactly and ask before ordering.

How do I know if my arched window frame is out of square?

Measure the diagonals.

For a rectangular lower section, measure:

  1. Bottom left corner to upper right corner
  2. Bottom right corner to upper left corner

If the two diagonal measurements differ by more than 1/2 inch, the frame is considered out of square.

Other signs include:

  • Uneven gaps around the frame
  • Cracks near the corners
  • A sill that slopes noticeably
  • Trim that has separated
  • Water staining
  • Difficulty opening nearby operable windows
  • Visible sagging above the window

An out-of-square frame does not always mean the project is doomed. It simply means the opening needs a better plan. Sometimes that means custom sizing. Sometimes it means full-frame replacement. Sometimes it means repairing the rough opening before installing the new window.

Conclusion

Measuring an arched window is not hard, but it does require patience. The most important steps are measuring the base width, center height, jamb depth, and diagonals, then confirming whether you have a perfect arch or a specialty shape.

If your window is a perfect arch, the math is straightforward: height equals half the width. If it is elongated, quarter-round, eyebrow-shaped, or out of square, take extra measurements and create a physical template before ordering.

With more than 30 years of experience and HOVER 3D visualization, we can help you see the finished result before work begins.
