meta: As the cold, snowy months quickly approach in Utah, it is important to take time to prepare your home’s exteriors for winter.
h1: How To Prepare Your Home’s Exteriors For Winter
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
As the cold, snowy months quickly approach in Utah, it is important to take time to prepare your home’s exteriors for winter.

Getting your home winter-ready may not be on the top of your to-do list. But, the reality is, you cannot procrastinate these tasks if you want your home to be prepared and protected throughout the next season. Snow, ice, wind, and other cold-weather elements can do serious damage to your home unless you dedicate the time, efforts, and resources to getting ready before the winter frost presents itself.

Keep scrolling to learn more about preparing your home’s exteriors for winter below.

Inspect Your Roof

Before the major snowstorms hit, it’s essential to know that your home does not have a leaky roof. A quick and simple roof inspection can help you locate any potential problems. Here’s what to keep your eye out for:

  • Curling Shingles — As you inspect your roof, keep your eyes open for curling shingles and other signs of damage. The sooner you fix these areas, the better.
  • Stains or Wet Spots — Stains and wet spots are obvious signs of leaks, leading to water damage and mold. Before it becomes a significant issue, make sure to have these areas repaired.
  • Signs of Critters — Watch for nests, animal droppings, and signs of gnawed-on wood and wires. It’s important to figure out how these pesky animals are entering your home. Not to mention, they can cause serious structural damage to your home over time.

Trim Nearby Tree Branches

Between heavy snowfall and intense wind, tree branches don’t stand much of a chance during winter. Before heavy snow-laden branches or knocked over trees damage your home, make sure to trim any threatening tree branches near your house.

Clean out Your Gutter System

Autumn brings many wind and rainstorms that can clog your gutters and downspouts in no time. If your gutter system is not thoroughly cleaned out before the next season, the low winter temps can cause ice dams that lead to extensive repairs. Now that the Utah leaves have all but fallen make sure to clean out your gutter to remove leaves, nests, twigs, and other debris. Additionally, make sure to inspect your gutter system to make sure it is in good working condition. Look out for areas that are sagging or leaking. If you find areas that need attention, make sure to address them right away. A professional can take care of these issues with no problem at all.

Make Repairs to Your Home’s Exteriors

If the siding on your home is damaged, it’s crucial to get them repaired right away. Areas left unfixed can lead to further problems, such as water damage and unwelcome furry visitors. Siding can certainly be repaired during any time of year, but it is best repaired before winter hits.

Contact M & M Gutters & Exteriors

Winterizing and preparing the exterior of your home should be your number one priority this winter season. If your siding, gutters, or other exterior needs attention this winter, contact the experts at M & M Gutters & Exteriors. Whether you live in Ogden or Provo, our team of knowledgeable and experienced professionals can get your Northern Utah home winterized and ready for all that Mother Nature throws your way. Contact us today.

title: How To Prepare Your Siding & Gutters for Fall | M&M Gutters
meta: Prepare your siding and gutters for the fall season with expert tips from M&M Gutters to avoid common issues and possible damage.
h1: How to Prepare Your Siding and Gutters for Fall
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Fall is only a few weeks away, and now is the perfect time to prepare your siding and gutters for the upcoming season.

Your exterior siding and gutter system can take an intense beating from the wide range of elements they experience throughout the summer. They could both use a little TLC, and, with a bit of elbow grease, they will be ready for the fall season.

Learn more about fall preparation for your exterior siding and gutter system below.

How to Prepare Your Siding for Fall

Get your siding ready for fall by doing the following:

Clean Siding Thoroughly — Spray and gently scrub away any dirt, mildew, and other caked-on debris from your siding. Make sure to check the small crevices for spider webs and nests to avoid critters permanently moving into your space once the colder months settle in.

Inspect Siding and Make Repairs — Take a good look at your sliding. Look for cracks, missing pieces, or damaged areas. Make sure to repair any areas necessary to avoid air leaks (which can lead to increased utility bills) and water damage.

Trim Trees and Plants — Shrubs, trees, and other plants too close to your home can cause serious damage during fall and winter storms. While siding was made to stand up to moisture from snow, ice, and rain, it might not do so well if a tree branch were to break and fall on your house.

Clean Gutters — When gutters and downspouts aren’t clear of debris, water can overflow and run down your siding. Over time, this can cause water damage and other adverse impacts on your home.

How to Prepare Your Gutters for Fall

Here’s what you can do to get your gutter system fall-ready:

Clean Gutters — Before you store your hose for the season, use it to spray out your gutters. Clear away all debris and any clogs to ensure your gutters can whisk away water effectively. Grab a bucket and gloves for extra stubborn areas and clean it out by hand. For more information on unclogging your gutters, check out this post.

Inspect and Repair Gutters — While cleaning your gutters, inspect your system for any signs of damage. Look for sagging or uneven areas, loose brackets or screws, and any other wear and tear. Make repairs as soon as you notice they are needed. Ignoring damaged gutters for too long can lead to more permanent damage.

Install Gutter Guards — In addition to trimming trees, shrubs, and other plants, add gutter guards to your system to help prevent clogs and build up. Not only will guards keep out leaves and other debris, but they’ll also prevent unwanted mice and other creatures from moving in. Learn more about gutter guards here.

Contact M & M Gutters & Exteriors

We service Salt Lake, Davis, Utah, Weber, and Summit counties. Contact M & M Gutters & Exteriors today for your siding or gutter needs.

title: How To Prevent Ice Dams - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: They can harm your home in various ways, including tearing off your gutter system. Prevent ice dams effectively with proven strategies from M&M Gutters, protecting your home during winter.
h1: How To Prevent Ice Dams
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Icicles hanging along your roofline are a dreamy, picturesque sight; however, they can lead to troublesome problems like ice dams.

Ice dams are thick ridges of cold, solid ice that build up along the eaves of your house. They can harm your home in various ways, including tearing off your gutter system, loosen shingles, and cause water to back up and leak in through your roof. The effects of these dams, as you can imagine, are not pretty: warped walls and floors, peeling paint, and sagging ceilings — not to mention the unseen water damage and mold this can cause inside of your walls.

As you can see, dams are a major problem you want to avoid. Thankfully, there are things you can do to prevent them. Continue reading to learn how.

Preventing Ice Dams

Chipping and chiseling away at the dams on your eaves is bad for your roof (and dangerous!), and sprinkling salt on them will actually do more harm to the shrubbery and vegetation below than to the dams. Outside of wishing away the freezing temperatures, you can do one other thing to prevent dams: heated cables.

Heated cables, also called ice melting systems, are attached to your roof’s edge using clips in a zig-zag pattern that helps prevent these dams from forming and harming your roofing and gutters and creating serious hazards on the ground below. Heated cables allow you to equalize the temperature of your roof by heating it from the outside versus other, less effective methods. It is ideal to have an ice melting system installed before the freezing temps and snow hit.

What to Do if They Have Already Formed

If an ice dam has already formed, there are a few things you can do yourself to try to remediate the issue:

Blow Cold Air — Head to your attic and aim a box fan at the underside of the roof where the leaky is occurring. This concentrated air will freeze the water in minutes and will stop the water in its tracks.

Ventilate Your Ridge and Eaves — Air can best circulate when your ridge and soffits are vented and help reduce these dams.

Rake It Off — Grab your favorite long-handled roof rake and remain safely on the ground with a good stance. Carefully begin removing snow and enjoy the falling snow around you. Just make sure to bundle up and use caution!

Add More Insulation — Keep the heat where it belongs by adding more insulation to the attic floor. Find out how much your attic needs by checking with your local building department.

Contact M & M Gutters

Protect your Utah home and gutter system by preventing ice dams with an ice melting system from M & M Gutters. Our self-regulating heat tape prevents icicles and ice dams from forming altogether. By automatically adjusting the power output to accommodate any changes in outside air temperature, our system delivers the exact amount of heat necessary to prevent ice and ice damage. Contact our experts today! We serve Salt Lake County, Utah.

title: Preventing Roof Damage During Utah Winters - M&M Gutters
meta: How do you keep your roof safe from heavy snow and ice? Below are ten helpful tips to prepare your roof for Utah’s harsh winters.
h1: How To Prevent Roof Damage During Utah Winters
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
When winter shows up in Utah, it brings beautiful snow-covered mountains. However, it also
brings the risk of roof damage from ice. Some homes even experience roof collapse from snow.
So how do you keep your roof safe from heavy snow and ice? Below are ten helpful tips to
prepare your roof for Utah’s harsh winters.

1. How Do Heavy Snow Loads Affect My Roof?

Before diving into roof ice removal techniques, it’s essential to understand the potential damage
snow can cause. Ice dams and heavy snowfall can cause water to seep under shingles, causing
leaks and roof damage. But how much snow is too much for a roof? Ultimately, it depends on
the specific roof. However, the average roof can hold about 20 inches of packed snow or 40-45
inches of fresh snow.

2. Trim Your Tree Branches

One of the first things you can do to prevent roof damage from ice is to cut any overhanging tree
branches. Falling branches covered in snow can damage your shingles and gutters. Before
winter rolls in, trim back any tree branches close to your roof.

3. Clean Your Gutters

Clogged gutters can cause a lot of damage during winter. When leaves and debris build up in
your gutters, they obstruct water flow and create ice dams that cause water to back up under
your roof.

4. Remove Debris

Besides cleaning your gutters, removing debris from your roof is also a good idea. Leaves,
twigs, and other materials can trap moisture and cause roof decay. You can use a roof rake or
opt for a professional Salt Lake City roof cleaning company.

5. Insulate Your Attic

A well-insulated attic helps maintain a consistent temperature and prevents ice dams. Install
high-quality insulation to get your attic ready for the cold Utah winters.

6. Remove Snow Often as Possible

Remove snow as often as possible to prevent roof damage from ice and heavy snow loads.
However, be careful when removing snow because improper snow removal can damage
shingles and roofing materials. Consider hiring a professional for snow and ice removal from
your roof.

7. Repair Broken or Missing Shingles

Damaged or missing shingles can let water seep in and cause leaks. Before winter, inspect your
roof for any signs of damage and then repair them immediately.

8. Reseal Around Vents and Other Fixtures

The seals around your roof’s vents, skylights, and other fixtures can deteriorate over time.
Replacing or resealing these areas will protect your home during snowfalls.

9. Check Your Siding

Your siding is another area of your home that can be vulnerable during winter. To prevent water
from causing damage in your home, check your siding for any cracks, gaps, or signs of damage.

10. Install a Roof Ice Melt System

For additional help with ice removal from your roof, you can install a roof ice melt system. At
M&M Gutters, we offer an innovative system that prevents ice dams and keeps your roof safe
throughout the winter.

Potential Winter Problems if Your Roof Goes Unattended

Leaving your roof unattended can be a costly mistake. Here is some of the damage you could
face if you don’t properly prepare for winter.

Ice Dams

Ice dams are common during winter, especially in places like Utah that get a lot of snow. When
heat leaves your home, it warms the roof and melts the snow. The melted snow can refreeze
around the roof’s edges, forming ice dams. Without removal, ice dams prevent drainage, which
can cause water damage.

Heavy Snow Loads

Heavy snowfalls can put a lot of weight on your roof. Roofs are designed to hold a certain
amount of snow, but too much snow can cause structural damage.

Roof Leaks

Roof leaks are common if you don’t care for your roof. Leaks aren’t just an inconvenience —
they can also lead to extensive damage to your walls, ceilings, and insulation.

Shingle Damage

Cold temperatures and freezing can make shingles weak and crack. Heavy snow loads can also
put too much pressure on shingles and cause damage.

Condensation and Moisture

The difference in temperature between your home’s cold exterior and warm interior can cause
condensation in the attic. Condensation can lead to mold growth and wood rot, affecting your
home’s structural integrity and air quality.

Poorly Ventilated Attic

Improper ventilation in an attic can trap moisture, causing ice dams. Proper ventilation in your
attic is crucial in preventing moisture-related problems.

Roof Collapse

Roof collapse from snow is an issue some Utah homeowners face during the winter. Twenty
pounds of snow per square foot is usually how much weight a house roof can hold. Anything
heavier may cause a roof to collapse.

Ice and debris can clog gutters and downspouts, leading to overflowing gutters and potential
water damage to your home’s foundation.

h1: How To Properly Clean Vinyl Siding
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
With spring cleaning in full force, M&M Gutters has been busy helping dedicated homeowners wash away the grime of a long winter season. It’s a rewarding challenge to clean out gutters, spray out and organize garages, weed and fertilize your budding lawn and garden, and to wash windows and siding. Your home has likely taken a beating through our latest Utah winter, with snow, ice, wind, rain, and mud coming from all sides. Every house needs a good cleaning, and you’ll be shocked to see just how much grime and discoloration you’ve gotten used to on your home’s exterior.

Vinyl siding is popular because it is durable, affordable, and comes in a wide range of colors and designs. However, it isn’t invulnerable, and regular cleaning will keep pests and damage from weakening your vinyl siding. Pollen, droppings, rust, mold, and even insecticides and other chemical products you may use on your property can cause stains and discoloration in vinyl siding.

That’s why it’s critical to regularly clean your vinyl siding each spring. How To Properly Clean Vinyl Siding?

  1. Prepare. Walk around your home and remove any obstacles. You may take this opportunity to trim any shrubs, throw away trash, and look for any spots in your siding that may be in need of repair.
  2. Choose Your Cleaning Solution. There are many appropriate cleaning solutions for cleaning vinyl siding. The best and simplest cleaning solution for vinyl siding is 70% water 30% vinegar. This is natural, cheap, and effective. If you are worried about stains, mold, or a more dirty vinyl siding, you can combine half cups of powdered laundry detergent and house cleaner with a gallon of water and a few cups of bleach. If you have lots of landscaping and want to be plant-friendly, you can use oxygen bleach which will clean without harming any of your plants or landscaping.
  3. Consider Tools. At the very least you will need a bucket, rag or soft-bristled brush, and a ladder. If you want to make it more effective and efficient, you may consider cleaning your vinyl siding with a power washer. Try it on the lowest setting and be sure to spray in a direct line, not upward or an angle that will loosen your vinyl siding. For your final tool you might consider asking a family member or friend to assist you to make it faster, safer, and more fun!
  4. Go! Now that you are ready with tools and preparation, you can clean your vinyl siding. Choose a day with good weather, and be sure to thoroughly rinse any cleansing residue from your vinyl siding after it is clean. Take a before-and-after picture of your vinyl siding for maximum satisfaction!

title: Siding Maintenance: How To Remove Mold From Your Siding?
meta: There are several approaches to removing mold from siding. Here’s a look at some of the most effective ways to get rid of the mold on (or under) your siding
h1: How To Remove Mold From Your Siding
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
It’s no small task to remove mold from your siding, but it’s possible with the right tools and a lot of determination. Mold can grow just about anywhere that moisture is present, and the exterior of your home is exposed to moisture daily. This sneaky fungus might be growing on the visible outer side of your siding, but it can become much more dangerous when it grows underneath your siding.

There are several approaches to removing mold from siding, and what works in one home might not be right for another home. Here’s a look at some of the most effective ways to get rid of the mold on (or under) your siding.

Pressure Washing

One of the easiest options to remove mold from your siding is pressure washing it off. You can rent pressure washers from your local home improvement store or borrow one from a neighbor if you don’t have one of your own.

If you choose to use a pressure washer to remove mold, take extra care. Extreme water pressure applied incorrectly can cause serious damage to the siding, including dents, holes, and even removing the paint. Test your method on an inconspicuous area of siding first before moving to more obvious areas.

To start, you’ll need a mixture of hot water and a mold-killing agent. For the best results, use a cleaning solution that is made specifically for removing mold from the siding. Most of these cleaners will also keep mold from growing again for an extended period.

Once you’ve mixed your cleaner and added it to the pressure washer, you’re ready to clean. Set the pressure washer at the widest setting and step back so you’re standing several feet away. You can move forward and side to side as needed. Point the nozzle directly at the siding rather than at an angle.

It’s especially important not to spray water up at the siding since this can cause moisture to work its way underneath your siding and create a perfect environment for mold to grow hidden from view. Keep that nozzle straight ahead and work your way in sections left to right, top to bottom.

While mold might not be covering every inch of your siding, it’s a good idea to wash all of the siding anyway. Otherwise, you’ll end up with a very clean and shiny section and the rest of your home will look very dirty.

Pressure washing your siding is a great way to spruce up your house and improve your curb appeal, and it will help prevent mold from growing in the future since mold feeds on dirt and grime accumulation on the siding.

Homemade Vinegar Solution

Most commercial mold removing solutions are chemical based. So if you’re looking for something a little more environmentally friendly, try making your cleaning solution at home using one part distilled white vinegar to three parts hot water.

This cleaner is safe for most types of siding and is tough on mold. Keep in mind that this option isn’t as hands-off as pressure washing. With this cleaning solution, you’ll need to apply a serious amount of elbow grease. Find a good scrub brush and get to work, and be prepared for it to take a while. Just be sure to wear rubber gloves and protect your skin, face, and eyes from exposure to mold and vinegar.

Bleach

If the vinegar isn’t cutting it, but you still want to go with a homemade cleaning solution, bleach might be your best bet. Just make sure you remove every trace of the vinegar first since bleach and vinegar together make an extremely poisonous substance. Mix one gallon of hot water with a quart of bleach and a cup of powdered laundry detergent.

Use gloves and protect your clothes and other surfaces from drips. Use a soft sponge or a gentle scrub brush to work the mold off of the siding. Rinse the surface thoroughly after you finish.

Bleach can be an extremely powerful mold removal agent, but it comes with its share of hazards. It might not be safe on all types of siding, so be sure to test it in a less visible area before you move to more obvious areas.

How To Remove Mold Underneath Siding

It can be difficult to tell if you have mold growing underneath your siding because you can’t exactly look at it. But if you have mold on the outside, there’s a chance that some of it worked its way underneath.

If you do find that you have mold growing underneath your siding, there’s not a lot you can do on your own. Consult a mold removal specialist if you’re fully committed to keeping your existing siding. But the most effective method would be replacing your siding with something that will keep the moisture out more effectively and protect your home from future mold problems.

Whichever step you take, it’s important to address mold growth quickly. Mold feeds on organic materials like wood and drywall, so with enough time, the mold can compromise the structural integrity of your home. This can cause safety issues for your family and might also cause respiratory problems, allergies, and asthma.

title: How to Size Up Your Window Rough Opening Without Making Costly Mistakes - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Learn how to measure rough opening for replacement windows accurately with this guide to avoid costly sizing mistakes and ensure a perfect fit.
h1: How to Size Up Your Window Rough Opening Without Making Costly Mistakes
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
How to Measure a Window Opening Before You Order

First, decide what stays. For a full-frame replacement, expose and measure the rough opening between the wall framing. For an insert replacement, the old frame stays, so measure the clear space inside its jambs instead. From indoors, take three width measurements and three height measurements. Record the smallest of each, then check both diagonals and the available depth. Do not order from trim or glass measurements.

I’m Nathan Nuttall at M&M Gutters & Exteriors. From our team’s 30-plus years of exterior home improvement work in Utah, I’ll explain how to measure rough opening for replacement windows and when to have an installer check your numbers.

How to measure rough opening for replacement windows vocab explained:

  • how to measure a replacement window
  • how to measure double hung windows
  • how to measure vinyl replacement windows

Rough Opening vs. Frame Size: Choosing Insert vs. Full-Frame Replacements

Upgrading your home’s windows is one of the most rewarding investments you can make. In 2026, the average cost per replacement window sits at $477, with most projects ranging between $232 and $740 per unit. When undertaking a whole-house upgrade, homeowners typically invest an average of $7,354 (ranging between $3,440 and $11,840). The payoff is substantial: over 66% of homeowners report saving $25 to $100 per month on utility bills, while ENERGY STAR certified replacements can slash heating and cooling costs by $125 to $340 annually. Furthermore, homeowners recover up to 76% of their project costs at resale for vinyl window upgrades.

However, all of those efficiency and financial gains depend on one critical factor: ordering the correct size. A replacement window that is even 1/2 inch too wide will not fit into the wall, and one that is too small creates massive air gaps, structural instability, and potential water leaks. The cost of repairing water damage from a faulty window installation can quickly escalate from $2,000 to over $10,000.

Before touching a tape measure, you must understand the distinction between structural rough openings and existing frame dimensions, as well as whether your project calls for a pocket insert or a full tear-out.

Measuring the Structural Framing vs. Existing Window Frame

A true rough opening (RO) refers to the unfinished, framed structural opening in your wall surrounded by the wooden or steel framing members: the header on top, the rough sill at the bottom, and the trimmer/jack studs on either side.

In contrast, the existing window frame is the finished framework (head jamb, side jambs, and sill) that holds the operating window sashes.

  • Stud-to-Stud (Rough Opening): Measured across the raw framing lumber. This measurement is required for new construction windows or full-frame tear-outs.
  • Jamb-to-Jamb (Pocket Insert): Measured across the interior finished side jambs of the current window unit.

Never measure the decorative interior casing or exterior brickmould. Trim pieces fluctuate in thickness, style, and placement, and they do not reflect the physical structural space where your new unit must sit. When you want to capture perfect window dimensions, always run your tape directly against the structural wood or the bare jamb surfaces.

Pocket Insert vs. Full-Frame Tear-Out: What Your Opening Requires

Choosing the right installation method determines what you actually measure.

An insert replacement (often called a pocket replacement) slides a new, fully assembled window unit directly into the existing, sound wooden window frame. This approach preserves your interior trim, drywall, and exterior siding. It is faster, less intrusive, and budget-friendly.

A full-frame replacement involves stripping everything away—sashes, frame, interior casing, exterior trim, and flashing—until only the bare wall studs remain. While it adds approximately $150 to $300 per window to your total project cost, a full tear-out is necessary if:

  1. The existing frame shows signs of wood rot, moisture intrusion, or insect damage.
  2. The framing has racked or settled severely, throwing the opening heavily out of square.
  3. You want to maximize your glass viewable area or alter the overall window style.

Evaluating frame condition early prevents ordering errors and helps guide accurate replacement window sizing from day one.

The Complete Process: How to Measure Rough Opening for Replacement Windows

Whether you are measuring bare studs for a full-frame installation or measuring inside an existing jamb pocket for an insert, the fundamental technique follows the same strict, repeatable process.

Essential Tools and Preparation for How to Measure Rough Opening for Replacement Windows

To get reliable, repeatable numbers, set aside fabric sewing tapes or flexible promotional rulers. You will need:

  • A heavy-duty steel tape measure (1-inch wide blade prevents sagging over wide spans)
  • A 2-foot or 4-foot spirit level (or a reliable digital torpedo level)
  • An angle finder (optional, but helpful for bay/bow units)
  • A dedicated notepad or mobile worksheet
  • Safety glasses and a sturdy step ladder

Refer to a manufacturer-approved measurement guide for new construction and replacement windows (JMI003) to ensure your recorded dimensions align with industry standards before placing an order.

The Three-Measurement Rule for Accurate Width and Height

Houses settle over time due to seasonal humidity cycles and soil movement. As a result, window openings are almost never perfect rectangles. A single measurement taken across the middle is a recipe for disaster. Always follow the three-measurement rule:

1. Measuring Width (Three Points)

Open the window sash (or work within the bare studs) and measure horizontally across the opening:

  • Measure near the top (roughly 6 inches down from the top corners).
  • Measure across the exact middle.
  • Measure near the bottom (roughly 6 inches up from the sill).
  • Rule: Record all three, and highlight the smallest number.

2. Measuring Height (Three Points)

Measure vertically from the highest point of the sill to the top head jamb/header:

  • Measure along the left side (6 inches inward from the corner).
  • Measure directly down the center.
  • Measure along the right side (6 inches inward from the corner).
  • Rule: Record all three, and highlight the smallest number.

When ordering factory-built units, always round down to the nearest 1/8 inch. Rounding up even a fraction of an inch can leave you with a window that refuses to slide into the opening. These principles are especially critical when measuring vinyl replacement windows, as rigid vinyl frames cannot be planed down or trimmed on the job site.

Checking Squareness, Level, Plumb, and Jamb Depth

Once you have recorded your widths and heights, you must verify that the opening is square, level, plumb, and deep enough.

  1. The Diagonal Check (Squareness): Measure diagonally from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, then measure from the top-right corner to the bottom-left corner. Compare the two numbers.
    • If the two diagonal measurements differ by 1/4 inch or less, your opening is acceptably square for standard replacements.
    • If the difference exceeds 1/4 inch, the opening has “racked” into a parallelogram, requiring structural shimming or a full-frame rebuild.
  2. Level and Plumb: Place your level against the sill and both side jambs. The opening cannot be more than 1/8 inch out-of-level or plumb across its entire span.
  3. Checking Pocket Depth: For an insert window, measure the clear depth from the back edge of the interior stop moulding to the front edge of the exterior blind stop strip. A standard insert replacement requires a minimum pocket depth of 3-1/4 inches. If your depth is shallower than this, a standard pocket unit will protrude past your interior trim.

These checks are essential whether you are performing a double-hung window measurement or sizing modern casements.

Avoiding Expensive Mistakes: Clearances, Tolerances, and Ordering Rules

Ordering replacement windows involves specific clearance tolerances. Understanding how manufacturers use rough opening numbers versus net frame dimensions ensures your new windows fit smoothly and insulate properly.

Critical Tolerances and Clearance Calculations for Window Ordering

When dealing with a true rough opening (stud-to-stud), the industry standard clearance is 1/4 inch on each side (top, bottom, left, and right). This means:

  • The rough opening width should be 1/2 inch larger than the actual net window frame width.
  • The rough opening height should be 1/2 inch larger than the actual net window frame height.

This 1/2-inch total difference leaves adequate room for:

  • Square-and-plumb adjustments using cedar or composite shims.
  • Expansion and contraction of vinyl, composite, or fiberglass materials over Utah’s broad temperature swings.
  • Low-expansion polyurethane insulating foam to seal drafts around the perimeter.

When you provide dimensions to a window supplier, clarify whether you are giving them Rough Opening Dimensions or Net Frame Dimensions. If you specify rough opening, the factory will typically make the automatic 1/2-inch deduction. If you specify net frame size, they build to that exact measurement.

Additionally, always ensure your window dimensions comply with local municipal building regulations, such as the Summit County Building Department residential code guidelines for emergency escape and rescue openings.

Specialty Scenarios: How to Measure Rough Opening for Replacement Windows in Bays, Bows, and Basements

Standard rectangular openings are straightforward, but specialty architectural styles require extra steps:

  • Bay and Bow Windows: These multi-panel units project outward from your exterior wall. Never measure across the front curve as a single span. You must measure the width and height of each individual panel, calculate the projection depth from the exterior wall face, and determine the exact angle (typically 30, 45, or 90 degrees) of the flanking side units. Review our specific guide on measuring for bay and bow replacements before tackling these complex projects.
  • Basement Egress and Hopper Windows: Below-grade basement windows often sit directly against poured concrete or cinder block openings. In addition to standard width and height, you must account for the exterior window well clearance and verify that finished net clear opening dimensions meet modern municipal egress safety codes (minimum 5.7 sq. ft. net clear opening, minimum 20 inches width, 24 inches height). Learn more in our guide on hopper window installation.

Frequently Asked Questions About Window Measurement

Should you measure replacement windows from the inside or outside of the home?

You should measure replacement windows from the inside of your home in almost every circumstance. Interior measuring allows you to place your tape measure directly against the actual side jambs, head jamb, and sill without decorative exterior siding, storm windows, or brickmould obscuring the true frame. It is also significantly safer, eliminating the need to balance on high exterior extension ladders.

What should you do if the diagonal measurements differ by more than 1/4 inch?

If your diagonal measurements differ by more than 1/4 inch, your window opening is significantly out of square (racked). A standard pocket insert window will not operate properly in a severely racked opening—the sashes will bind, hardware will fail, and weatherstripping will not seal evenly. In this scenario, you should opt for a full-frame replacement, which allows your installer to expose the bare wall studs, re-shim the opening plumb and square, and correct any underlying framing settlement.

What is the minimum jamb depth required for an insert replacement window?

Standard vinyl and composite insert replacement windows require a minimum clear pocket depth of 3-1/4 inches. This measurement is taken between the backside of your interior trim stop and the interior edge of the exterior blind stop. If your existing frame depth is less than 3-1/4 inches, an insert unit will extend awkwardly past your interior drywall, meaning a full-frame replacement or custom trim build-out is required.

Conclusion

Measuring your window openings is an empowering first step in planning your home remodel. By taking three width and three height measurements, selecting the smallest dimension, checking diagonals for squareness, and verifying jamb depth, you can budget accurately and avoid expensive sizing blunders.

Because replacement window units are custom-built to the eighth of an inch and cannot be returned once manufactured, we always recommend having a trained professional conduct a final verification measurement before placing your custom factory order.

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, our team brings over three decades of exterior remodeling expertise to homeowners throughout Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County, Utah County, Davis County, Summit County, and Northern Utah. Using cutting-edge 3D visualization technology with HOVER, we help you design, measure, and install high-performance windows that keep your home comfortable in every season. Contact us today to explore our professional window replacement services and schedule your on-site measurement consultation!

title: How To Unclog A Rain Gutter - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
h1: How To Unclog A Rain Gutter
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Part of your regular home maintenance includes inspecting your rain gutter for debris that might be clogging your gutter. Water backs up when your rain gutter is obstructed, which leads to soil erosion and water damage to your home. It’s essential to clean your rain gutter at least twice a year to prevent leaves and twigs from building up in your system. If you’ve detected your gutter is clogged, you’ll need to unclog it quickly to avoid damage to your landscaping, home’s exterior, foundation, and gutters. Keep on reading to find out how you can unclog your rain gutter.

Determining if Your Gutter Is Clogged

The best time to perform a rain gutter inspection is after it rains because you’ll be able to see any noticeable signs of a clogged gutter. Check for the following clogged gutter symptoms:

  • Water sprays like a fountain from the gutter’s seams and elbow joints.
  • Water spills over the gutter’s edges.
  • Water can’t flow out of the bottom of your gutter’s downspout extensions.

If it doesn’t rain much in your area, you can still perform a biannual gutter inspection. Check for the following telltale signs of a clogged gutter:

  • The gutter is pulling away from the fascia, likely caused by excessive weight
  • Wet, moist, dirty siding beneath your gutter
  • Peeling paint on siding fascia
  • Dirt erosion directly below your gutter

If you’ve determined your rain gutter is clogged, you’ll need to pinpoint the exact location of the problem, which can present a challenge. Start by checking your gutter’s downspout cage, which is a water strainer designed to trap debris while allowing water to flow through. One of the most common downspout cage problems is that it’s prone to bending out of place.

Another problem your rain gutter might be experiencing is slipping gutter hangers and spikes, which sometimes slip away from the fascia and land inside the gutter. Misplaced hangers and spikes can block your gutters, which will trap twigs and leaves; this will clog your gutter as a result. Some homeowners have downspouts that descend below ground level, and it’s likely the clog is a result of a fractured underground pipe.

Unclogging Your Rain Gutter

If your downspout cage is causing your rain gutter clog, you’ll need to do the following:

  1. Remove the downspout cage and clean it.
  2. Remove all the accumulated debris stuck inside your rain gutter.
  3. If your cage is in good shape, reseat it into the downspout hole.
  4. If your cage is damaged, you’ll need to buy a replacement screen.

If loose hangers or spikes are clogging your rain gutter, you’re in luck because it’s an easy fix. Do the following:

  1. Rid your gutter of any debris.
  2. Reposition your gutter’s supports or repair them as needed.

Unfortunately, if your gutter’s problem is coming from an underground pipe, you won’t be able to fix the issue on your own. Treating a fractured underground pipe requires deep excavation, and you may not have the proper equipment to perform this task.

Perhaps it’s time to replace your home’s rain gutter system. M&M Gutters offers k-style rain gutters, half-round gutters, and copper gutters. Our expert team will determine which rain gutter is best for your home. Contact us today.

title: Install a Leaf Guard System Now! - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Enhance your gutter system's efficiency with a leaf guard system installation by M&M Gutters experts. Learn when it is best to install a system.
h1: Install a Leaf Guard System Now!
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
The shift in seasons is upon us and the autumn leaves are falling at a rapid rate, which means it’s time to install a leaf guard system on your gutters.

With the temperatures cooling down, the winds picking up, and the colorful leaves falling, we know that autumn is in full force. This also means that it’s time to tend to your gutter system once again. The fall season is an important time to give your gutters some TLC since winter is encroaching. It is also an ideal time to install gutter protection.

Learn more about why now is a great time to install a new leaf guard system below.

Install a Leaf Guard System Today

If you are beginning to cross off items on your autumn property maintenance checklist, you should put installing a leaf guard system at the top of your list. Here’s why fall is the perfect time to add a leaf guard system to your gutters:

Defend Your Home Against Falling Leaves and Other Debris — The biggest benefit that comes from leaf guards is the protection against leaves and other debris from entering. This is especially important in fall when the leaves are dropping from trees, and the wind sends them right into the gutters. Moreover, this is the time of year when animals, insects, and other small critters begin to make nests to hunker down for the season, and your gutters are a great place for tiny winter homes. This can cause a myriad of issues.

Avoid Expensive Clogs — The leaves, twigs, and other debris that are in your unprotected gutters do not always exit as easily as they entered, causing significant clogs. Clogged gutters cannot effectively or efficiently drain or direct water away from your home which can lead to serious problems around your property, such as leaking roof, damaged soffit and fascia, and more.

Lessens the Chance of Ice Buildup — With freezing temperatures, it’s only a matter of time before the stagnant water in your gutters turns to ice. This is incredibly hard on your gutter system, and the weight of the ice can pull your gutters away from your roofline.

Another Layer of Home Protection — There are many rainy days in autumn, and an effective gutter system is essential to avoid pooling water around the base of your home. Rainwater that is not diverted can result in foundational cracks and leaks in your basement.

Not Just Beneficial in Autumn — Yes, a leaf guard system is particularly helpful in autumn, but you’ll find that it is also beneficial year round. A leaf guard system will help protect your home, prevent clogs, and keep your gutters clean throughout the year, regardless of the season or time of year.

title: Is a Leaf Guard Worth It? - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Are leaf guards worth it? Evaluate the benefits of investing in a leaf guard for your gutters with insights from M&M Gutters.
h1: Is a Leaf Guard Worth It?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Gutters can quickly become one of the most annoying and dangerous items in your home, simply due to the maintenance and repair. A good, clean gutter can go unnoticed for years, operating as designed and keeping your roof and home free from water buildup.

Gutters provide proper drainage and trim for functional and design purposes. But once you start dealing with leaf buildup in fall and winter, you can start to feel the pain. It’s important that your gutters remain free and clear of debris, and buildup needs to be regularly removed to keep your roof safe.

Many homeowners invest in leaf guards to try to prevent this buildup and the grueling task of removing buildup. If you do end up with a mountain of leaves in your gutter, it can mean inching your ladder along the side of your home, climbing up and down to scrape out dead and congealed leaves from your gutter. Try not to fall!

Maybe leaf guards can help prevent this problem, but is it worth it? M&M Gutters can help you decide.

What is a Leaf Guard?

Leaf guards, also called gutter guards, gutter screens, or gutter covers, are insets that sit atop your gutter to prevent leaves and other debris from falling into your gutter from the air or traveling down the roof. There are two main styles – gutter guards and gutter screens.

A guard will sit atop your gutter and prevent things from entering the gutter (including water for the most part). A screen allows selective permeation, so water can get through but most sizes of debris are stopped by the screen which usually sits inside the gutter at the top.

Is a Leaf Guard Worth It?

Purchasing a leaf guard can be a significant expense and home upgrade, so it’s important to consider the factors that could make it worthwhile or a waste of money. Leaf guards have been shown to be relatively effective at keeping large leaves from entering your gutter.

However, smaller debris such as seed pods or tree needles can still find their way into the gutter. In fact, certain types of leaf guards are actually more difficult to clean than a standard gutter, and they still require maintenance. Simply installing a leaf guard does not mean you’re free from gutter maintenance forever, unfortunately.

Most homeowners will need to get their gutter professionally cleaned at least once a year, even if they own a leaf guard. If your home is two stories or higher, you should be hiring a professional regularly anyway, since that height is dangerous for an ambitious amateur to clean alone.

For many people looking to save money, it may actually be worth it to hire gutter professionals to come clean than to purchase the leaf guard and then have to clean it yourself.

However, a leaf guard still may be the right choice for you if you live in a heavily forested area or have lots of foliage or snow and ice in your yard. Our experts at M&M Gutters can help you determine exactly what your home needs for proper gutters and drainage.

h1: Is Leaf Guard a Scam or a Solution?
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors

Are Leaf Guard Complaints a Warning Sign You Shouldn’t Ignore?

Leaf guard complaints are more common than most homeowners realize before they sign on the dotted line. Here is a quick summary of what customers report most often:

  • Debris buildup on top of the mesh, causing water to overflow instead of entering the gutter
  • Ice dams and icicles forming in cold climates, sometimes 3-6 feet long
  • Overflow on steep roofs and valleys, even in moderate rainfall
  • Pushy, high-pressure sales tactics and quotes that drop sharply after a customer tries to cancel
  • Warranty loopholes that exclude installation defects, ice damage, and mesh clogging
  • Poor customer service, including missed appointments and unreturned calls
  • Bird and pest nesting inside gutter systems despite “maintenance-free” promises

These are not isolated incidents. Major national gutter guard providers have accumulated hundreds of BBB complaints in recent years, with a significant portion remaining unresolved. One prominent brand even reached a multi-million dollar class action settlement in 2023 over claims its products were defective and misleadingly marketed as maintenance-free.

The promise of never cleaning your gutters again sounds great. And for some homeowners, gutter guards genuinely do help. But the gap between what is marketed and what is delivered is wide enough to cause real damage — to your home and your wallet.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors, and after more than 30 years serving Utah homeowners, I’ve seen the aftermath of poorly installed or underperforming gutter protection systems — which is exactly why understanding leaf guard complaints before you buy matters so much. Read on for an honest breakdown of what’s going wrong in this industry and how to protect yourself.

Common leaf guard complaints vocab:

  • Gutter guards Salt Lake City
  • Gutter guards near me
  • Professional gutter guard installation

Common Gutter Guard Complaints and Performance Issues

When we talk to homeowners in Salt Lake County or Davis County, the most frequent leaf guard complaints we hear involve the simple fact that the product doesn’t do what the glossy brochure promised. The “maintenance-free” dream often turns into a maintenance nightmare.

One of the biggest technical issues is surface tension. Many gutter guards, especially reverse-curve (hooded) designs, rely on water “clinging” to the metal to wrap around into the gutter. However, as dirt, pollen, and shingle oils accumulate on that surface, the water loses its grip. Instead of flowing into the gutter, it shoots right over the edge, creating a waterfall that can erode your landscaping or flood your basement.

Debris buildup is another major pain point. While the guards might keep large leaves out of the inside of the gutter, those leaves often just sit on top of the guard. This creates a “shelf” that blocks water entirely. Pine needles and maple seeds are notorious for getting stuck in the mesh or under the hood, requiring you to get on a ladder anyway—the very thing you paid thousands of dollars to avoid.

Beyond just leaves, animals can also cause you gutter problems. We’ve seen everything from bird nests to wasp colonies tucked inside the cozy, protected space provided by hooded gutter guards. In fact, some installers have reported finding dozens of bee nests in a single run of curved gutters.

Marketing ClaimReal-World Performance Issue
“Never clean your gutters again”Pollen and silt require regular hosing off to prevent “matting.”
“Handles the heaviest rainfall”Water often overshoots the gutter on steep roofs or in valleys.
“Lifetime No-Clog Warranty”Often only covers the inside of the gutter, not the surface blocking water.
“Adds value to your home”Poorly installed systems can cause fascia rot and ice damage.

So, do-gutter-leaf-guards-work? They can, but only if they are the right type for your specific roof and are installed by professionals who understand local weather patterns.

Why Do Customers Report Gutter Guard Complaints Regarding Overflow?

Overflow is perhaps the most frustrating of all leaf guard complaints. You spend $10,000 on a system, only to watch water pour over your front porch during a summer thunderstorm. This usually happens for three reasons:

  1. Steep Roof Pitches: In areas like Summit County or the bench of the Wasatch Front, many homes have steep roofs. Water gains incredible speed as it moves down the shingles. Many gutter guards simply can’t “catch” water moving that fast.
  2. Valley Water Volume: Roof valleys funnel a massive amount of water into a small area. Without high-flow diverters or specific modifications, a standard leaf guard will be overwhelmed instantly.
  3. Vertical Water Intake Failures: If a guard doesn’t have a high enough “intake” capacity, it acts more like a roof extension than a gutter.

For homeowners looking for clog-free-living-top-gutter-guard-solutions-in-salt-lake-city, it’s vital to choose a system that can handle the specific pitch and water volume of your home.

Dealing with Ice Dams and Frozen Gutters

In Northern Utah, we don’t just deal with rain; we deal with heavy snow and the dreaded freeze-thaw cycle. A common theme in leaf guard complaints is that these systems can actually make ice dams worse.

When ice builds up at the edge of your roof, a gutter guard provides a cold metal platform for that ice to latch onto. Instead of snow melting and flowing away, it freezes on the guard, creating massive icicles. We have seen reports of icicles 3 to 6 feet long hanging from gutter guards, posing a serious safety hazard to anyone walking below.

Furthermore, if your attic is losing heat, that heat melts the bottom layer of snow on your roof. That water then hits the cold gutter guard and freezes instantly. This can back up under your shingles, leading to interior water damage. While some companies claim their guards prevent this, the reality is that any physical barrier in the gutter can become a “prison” for ice.

When asking is-a-leaf-guard-worth-it, Utah residents must consider the winter performance. We often recommend integrated heat cables to mitigate these issues, but many national franchises don’t include these in their standard high-pressure sales quotes.

Analyzing Sales Tactics, Pricing, and Warranty Loopholes in the Gutter Protection Industry

If you’ve ever invited a national gutter guard company to your home, you might have experienced what many call “the four-hour presentation.” This is a major source of leaf guard complaints.

Many of these companies use aggressive sales tactics. They might start with an astronomical quote—sometimes as high as $30,000 for a standard home—and then miraculously “find” discounts if you agree to sign right then and there. We’ve seen cases where a $12,000 quote was slashed to $6,000 the moment the homeowner tried to walk away. This “used car salesman” approach is designed to pressure you into a decision before you can research the product’s flaws.

But the real trouble often starts after the check clears. Many homeowners find that the “Lifetime Warranty” is riddled with exclusions. Common loopholes include:

  • Environmental Factors: The company may refuse to service a clog if it’s caused by “excessive” oak tassels or pine needles, claiming these are unusual conditions.
  • Maintenance Requirements: Some warranties are voided if you don’t “professionally” clean the outside of the guards every year.
  • Installation Defects: If the original franchise goes out of business, the national brand may refuse to honor the warranty for installation-related leaks.

Before you buy, it is essential to ask are-gutter-guards-worth-the-investment-unpacking-the-price-tag. Often, the “premium” price you pay goes toward massive national advertising budgets and sales commissions rather than high-quality materials.

Understanding the Impact of Gutter Guard Complaints on Industry Reputation

The sheer volume of leaf guard complaints on sites like the Better Business Bureau (BBB) and Trustpilot has tarnished the reputation of the entire industry. Some of the largest national providers, for instance, have consumer ratings as low as 2.1 out of 5, with a majority of reviews being 1-star.

Common themes in these reviews include:

  • Service Delays: Customers waiting weeks or months for a technician to fix a leak.
  • No-Shows: Appointments scheduled and then ignored by the company.
  • Misleading Marketing: Claims that the product is “maintenance-free” when it clearly requires regular attention.

When you look at what-are-the-pros-and-cons-of-leaf-gutters, it’s clear that while the idea is sound, the execution by many national brands leaves much to be desired.

How to Choose a Reliable Gutter Protection System

So, are all gutter guards a scam? Not at all. But you have to know what to look for to avoid becoming another statistic in leaf guard complaints.

In our experience at M&M Gutters & Exteriors, the most effective systems are typically stainless steel micro-mesh. Unlike hooded systems that rely on surface tension, micro-mesh allows water to drop straight through while blocking even the smallest debris, like pine needles and shingle grit.

Here is what we recommend looking for:

  1. Surgical Grade Stainless Steel: This won’t rust or degrade over time.
  2. No Shingle Interference: Avoid systems that slide under your shingles, as this can void your roof warranty and cause leaks.
  3. Professional, Local Installation: Choose a company that lives in your climate. A guy in a call center in another state doesn’t understand Salt Lake City snow loads.

Choosing what-are-the-best-leaf-guards-for-gutters involves looking at the technical specs, not just the TV commercials. You want a system that is part of a seamless-protection-the-ins-and-outs-of-professional-gutter-guard-installation.

Even with the best system, you need to understand the how-to-clean-a-leaf-guard process. Usually, this just involves a quick spray with a garden hose once or twice a year to remove pollen or dust that can block the mesh.

Frequently Asked Questions about Gutter Guards

Do gutter guards cause roof damage or void warranties?

This is a major concern for homeowners. Many national brands install their products by prying up the bottom row of shingles and sliding the guard underneath. This can break the sealant bond of your shingles, making them susceptible to wind damage. In many cases, this will void your roof manufacturer’s warranty.

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we prefer fascia-mounted systems or those that attach to the gutter itself without disturbing the roofline. When considering can-leaf-guards-be-installed-on-existing-gutters, always ask exactly how they will be attached.

Are there specific gutter guard complaints for Utah homeowners?

Yes. In Salt Lake City and surrounding areas, the biggest complaints are:

  • Snow Weight: Cheap plastic guards often collapse under the weight of a heavy Utah snowstorm.
  • Pine Needles: Many systems that claim to block “everything” fail miserably when it comes to the thin needles from our local pine and fir trees.
  • Freeze-Thaw Damage: The constant melting and refreezing can pull gutters away from the house if the guards aren’t structurally sound.

What steps should I take if my gutter guards fail?

If you’re already dealing with leaf guard complaints like overflow or leaks, here is your game plan:

  1. Document Everything: Take photos and videos of the failure while it’s raining.
  2. Check Your Contract: Look for the specific “Service Request” procedures.
  3. Contact the BBB: If the company ignores you, filing a formal complaint often gets a faster response.
  4. Professional Inspection: Have a local expert (like us) take a look. Sometimes a simple pitch adjustment can fix the problem.

And remember, you should check do-you-still-need-to-clean-gutters-with-leaf-guards—the answer is almost always a “yes,” even if it’s just a light rinse.

Conclusion

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we’ve spent 30 years helping Salt Lake City homeowners navigate the “wild west” of home improvements. We’ve seen the leaf guard complaints firsthand, and we’ve made it our mission to provide solutions that actually work in the unique Utah climate.

We don’t believe in high-pressure sales or “magic” products. We believe in high-quality materials, expert installation, and being there for our neighbors when they need us. Whether you’re in Salt Lake, Utah County, or up in Weber, we offer a one-stop solution for gutters, roofing, and more. We even use 3D visualization technology with HOVER so you can see exactly how your new system will look before we ever pick up a hammer.

Don’t let your home become another cautionary tale. If you’re ready for a gutter system that is a solution rather than a scam, install-a-leaf-guard-system-now with the team that knows Utah best. Reach out to us today for a transparent, honest quote.

title: Keep Bugs Out: Accurately Measuring for Replacement Window Screens - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Learn how to measure for replacement window screens accurately with our step-by-step guide, tools, tips & common mistakes to avoid.
h1: Keep Bugs Out: Accurately Measuring for Replacement Window Screens
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
The Right Fit Starts Here: How to Measure for Replacement Window Screens

How to measure for replacement window screens comes down to a few simple steps most homeowners can do in under 15 minutes with a tape measure and a notepad.

Quick answer:

  1. Remove the existing screen from the window frame.
  2. Measure the width from outside edge to outside edge of the frame — measure at the top and bottom, use the smaller number.
  3. Measure the height from outside edge to outside edge — measure at the left and right sides, use the smaller number.
  4. Measure the frame depth (thickness) from the side — typically 5/16″, 3/8″, or 7/16″.
  5. Record all three numbers (width × height × depth) to the nearest 1/16 inch.
  6. If no screen exists, measure the window channel opening and subtract 1/8 inch from both width and height for proper fit.

A poorly fitted screen doesn’t just look bad — it lets bugs in. And window screens aren’t built to last forever. The average screen lasts about 15 years, depending on weather exposure, cleaning, and handling. When it’s time for a replacement, getting the measurement right the first time saves you money and frustration.

The good news? This is a very doable DIY task — as long as you know where to measure and what numbers to record.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors, and after more than 30 years helping Utah homeowners with exterior projects — including windows — I’ve seen how a simple measurement mistake can turn a quick fix into a costly headache. In this guide, I’ll walk you through exactly how to measure for replacement window screens so you get it right the first time.

Easy how to measure for replacement window screens word list:

  • How to Measure Double Hung Windows
  • How to Measure House Windows for Replacement

Essential Tools and Preparation for Measuring Window Screens

Before we dive into the “how-to,” we need to make sure you have the right gear. Accuracy is the name of the game here. A difference of just 1/8 inch can be the gap that lets a family of mosquitoes into your living room. Window screens are a critical component of home maintenance, especially in the varied climate of Northern Utah.

The Gear You’ll Need

  • Steel Tape Measure: Leave the cloth sewing tape in the drawer. You need a high-quality metal tape measure. A properly calibrated one is accurate within 1/64 inch, which is exactly the kind of precision we’re looking for.
  • Notepad and Pencil: You will be taking multiple measurements (top, middle, bottom). Don’t trust your memory!
  • Step Ladder: If you’re measuring windows from the outside or have tall windows, stay safe and use a sturdy ladder.
  • Putty Knife or Flathead Screwdriver: These are handy for gently prying out old, stubborn screens without damaging the window frame.

Preparing Your Workspace

Start by clearing away any curtains, blinds, or decorations that might block your access. If you’re working on the second story of your Salt Lake County home, decide if it’s safer to measure from the inside or outside. While measuring from the outside is often more accurate for a snug fit, safety always comes first.

Before you start measuring the screen itself, it’s a great idea to check the window for overall health. If your windows are difficult to open or show signs of rot, you might be dealing with more than just a screen issue. Check out our guide on Measuring Up: How to Get Perfect Window Dimensions Every Time to see if your window frames are still square and level.

Removing Old Screens Safely

To remove a screen from the inside, open the window fully. Look for pull tabs, pins, or springs. Usually, you’ll lift the screen up into the top track and pull the bottom toward you. If you’re outside, start at a lower corner and use your putty knife to gently dislodge the frame. Be careful not to bend the aluminum frame if you plan on using it as a template!

How to Measure for Replacement Window Screens Using an Existing Frame

If your old screen is still mostly intact (even if the mesh is torn), your job just got a lot easier. The most reliable way to get a replacement is to measure the existing frame. This is often referred to as the “outside-to-outside” method.

The Golden Rule: Width First, Height Second

In the window industry, we always list dimensions as Width x Height.

  1. Measure the Width: Lay the screen flat. Measure from the outside edge of the aluminum frame to the opposite outside edge. Do this at the top and the bottom. Why both? Screens can bow or warp over time. If the numbers differ, use the smaller measurement.
  2. Measure the Height: Measure from the very top edge to the very bottom edge. Do this on both the left and right sides. Again, if they differ, record the smaller number.
  3. Measure Frame Thickness: This is a step many DIYers skip, but it’s vital. Turn the screen sideways and measure the depth of the metal frame. In the U.S., there are three standard sizes that cover about 90% of windows.

For more details on this specific technique, you can read our Measure Twice, Screen Once: A Foolproof Method for Replacement Screens blog post.

Standard Frame Thicknesses

Knowing your window material can help you identify the right frame thickness:

Window MaterialStandard Screen Frame Thickness
Vinyl Windows5/16 inch
Aluminum Windows3/8 inch
Wood Framed Windows7/16 inch

Step-by-Step: How to Measure for Replacement Window Screens

When you are recording these numbers, precision is key. We recommend measuring to the nearest 1/16 inch.

  • Avoid Rounding Up: If your measurement is between 24 1/8″ and 24 3/16″, it is better to stay on the smaller side. A screen that is 1/16″ too small will still stay in the track; a screen that is 1/16″ too big simply won’t fit.
  • Check the Corners: Measure near the corners rather than the middle. Aluminum frames can bow inward over 15 years of Utah sun and snow, which might give you a “false” smaller reading in the center.

Identifying and Measuring Screen Hardware

Your screen isn’t just mesh and metal; it usually has hardware to keep it in place. You need to note what kind you have and where it sits.

  • Tension Springs: These are flat or coiled metal pieces usually at the top or side. They “squish” to let the screen pop into the track.
  • Pull Tabs: These are plastic or metal loops used to pull the screen out of the frame.
  • Crossbars: On full-height screens, a horizontal bar is often added for strength. If you need a crossbar, measure from the bottom of the frame to the center of the bar.

When ordering, you’ll need to specify the hardware location. We usually measure this “center-to-center” from the nearest corner.

Measuring for New Screens When the Original is Missing

What if the previous homeowner took the screens with them, or a windstorm sent them flying across Tooele County? Don’t panic. You can measure the window opening directly.

Finding the “U-Shaped Lip”

Look at your window frame. You should see a dedicated channel or a U-shaped lip where the screen is meant to sit. This is your target.

  1. Measure the Width: Place the end of your tape measure inside the screen track on the left and measure across to the inside of the track on the right.
  2. Measure the Height: Measure from the bottom sill track to the top header track.
  3. The 1/8-Inch Rule: This is the most important part of how to measure for replacement window screens when no screen is present. You must subtract 1/8 inch from your total width and height. This provides “play” or clearance so you can actually maneuver the screen into the tracks without forcing it.

For a deeper dive into window anatomy, check out our How to Measure Replacement Windows Guide.

Pro Tips for a Snug Fit

  • Vertical vs. Horizontal: On some windows, you measure from the vertical lip to the channel. If you’re measuring a window with a deep groove on one side (common in horizontal sliders), put the tape all the way into the deep groove, measure to the opposite edge, and then subtract your clearance.
  • Adding vs. Subtracting: Some manufacturers suggest adding 1/8 inch to the height if you are measuring from the lip to the sash. However, the safest bet for most DIY orders is to measure the maximum opening and subtract 1/8 inch for clearance.
  • Check for Squareness: Measure the diagonals of the window opening (top left to bottom right, and top right to bottom left). If the two numbers differ by more than 1/4 inch, your window is “out of square.” In this case, you might need a professional to help with a custom fit. Read more in The Double-Hung Window Measurement Handbook: No More Guesswork.

Accounting for Window Types and Hardware Variations

Not all windows are created equal, and neither are their screens. The style of window you have in your Davis County or Weber County home will dictate what kind of screen you need.

Double-Hung and Single-Hung Windows

These usually use half screens that cover only the bottom sash. They typically slide into tracks and are held in place by tension springs at the top.

Horizontal Sliders

These also use half screens, but they move side-to-side. One side of the window frame often has a deeper “pocket” or groove. You’ll want to seat the screen in that deep groove first, then pull it back into the shallower track on the other side.

Casement and Awning Windows

Because these windows crank outward, the screens are located on the inside. These screens often use “plunger bolts” or “butterfly latches” to lock into the interior frame.

Choosing Your Mesh Type

Since you’re replacing the screen anyway, consider upgrading the mesh:

  • Standard Fiberglass: The most common and affordable. It’s flexible and won’t dent like aluminum.
  • Pet-Resistant Screen: If you have a cat that likes to climb or a dog that paws at the window, this mesh is up to 7x stronger than standard fiberglass.
  • Solar Protection: Great for south-facing windows in Utah’s hot summers. These can block up to 65-90% of UV rays, keeping your home cooler and protecting your furniture from fading. According to Energy.gov, solar screens are most effective on windows that receive direct sunlight.

Need help identifying your window style? We’ve got a guide for that: Different Window Styles for Your Home.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Measuring Window Screens

Even with the best intentions, mistakes happen. Here are the “don’ts” we see most often at M&M Gutters & Exteriors:

  1. Measuring the Glass Only: This is the #1 mistake. The screen frame sits in the window frame, not against the glass. Always measure the tracks or the old screen frame.
  2. Ignoring the Depth: If you buy a 7/16″ thick screen for a track designed for 5/16″, it simply won’t slide in.
  3. Measuring Only One Side: Windows settle. Frames bow. Always measure top/bottom and left/right. Use the smallest measurement to ensure the screen fits.
  4. Forgetting Hardware: If your window requires tension springs to stay in, and you order a screen without them, it will rattle or fall out during the first Northern Utah canyon wind.
  5. Assuming All Windows are the Same: Even if two windows look identical, measure them both. In many homes, “standard” sizes can vary by 1/8 inch from room to room.

If you find that your screens are constantly falling out or your windows are drafty, it might be a sign that the windows themselves are failing. Take a look at 11 Signs You Need New Windows for Your Home to see if it’s time for an upgrade.

Frequently Asked Questions about Window Screens

Should I measure the screen or the window opening?

If you have the old screen and it fit well, measure the screen frame (outside-to-outside). It is the most accurate template. If the screen is missing or badly bent, measure the window opening tracks and subtract 1/8 inch for clearance.

How precise do my measurements need to be?

You should measure to the nearest 1/16 inch. While 1/8 inch is often acceptable, 1/16 inch ensures a “professional” fit with no gaps for tiny gnats or “no-see-ums” to get through.

Why do I need to subtract 1/8 inch from my measurements?

Screens need a tiny bit of “wiggle room” to be installed. If the screen is the exact same size as the opening, the friction will make it nearly impossible to slide into the tracks without scratching the paint or bending the screen frame.

Conclusion

Learning how to measure for replacement window screens is a fantastic way to maintain your home’s comfort and curb appeal. By following the “measure twice, order once” rule and paying close attention to your frame thickness and hardware, you can keep the fresh air in and the Utah bugs out.

However, we know that life gets busy, and sometimes windows in older homes in Salt Lake City or Summit County can be tricky. If your windows are out of square, or if you’re looking to replace the windows entirely for better energy efficiency, we are here to help.

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we bring over 30 years of experience to every project. We don’t just do gutters; we are your one-stop shop for roofing, siding, and Windows. We even use HOVER 3D visualization technology so you can see exactly how your new windows and screens will look before we ever pull out a tool.

Ready for a perfect fit? Check out our guide on the Best Windows for Your Utah Home or contact us today for a professional consultation. Whether you’re in Salt Lake County or Weber County, we’ve got you covered!
