If you want to add the best leaf guards to your home, contact the experts at M & M Gutters & Exteriors! We’ll provide the highest quality gutters and exteriors for your house. Whatever your needs are, no request is too big or too small for our experienced team. Call our professionals to learn which system is best suited for your home. We serve Salt Lake, Davis, Weber, Utah, and Summit counties in Utah.

title: What are the Pros of Leaf Gutters & Cons of Leaf Guards?
meta: Here’s a look at everything you need to know about various leaf solutions for your rain gutters, including the Pros of Leaf Gutter and the Cons of Leaf Guards.
h1: What are the Pros and Cons of Leaf Gutters?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Leaf gutters can be a real game-changer for those who tend to neglect their rain gutters until they can no longer serve their purpose. They can also save homeowners hours of work during spring cleaning.

But if you don’t already have a leaf filter on your gutters, you might be wondering if it’s really worth the cost of purchasing gutters and having them professionally installed.

Here’s a look at everything you need to know about various leaf solutions for your rain gutters, including the pros and the cons.

How Do Leaf Gutters Work?

Leaf gutters come in several different varieties, but they all serve the same purpose: to keep the leaves and debris out while still allowing water through. Most leaf solutions consist of a leaf filter that sits on top of or just inside your gutters and filters out the debris as the water runs off your roof.

There are five primary types of leaf guards: screen, micro-mesh, reverse curve or surface tension, brush, and foam. Screen guards are the cheapest and easiest to install, while reverse curve gutters tend to be the most popular.

The proper guards for your home will depend on your environment and the type of gutters you have installed in your home. Consult a professional before choosing a type of gutter guard, and have them install them for you.

Pros of Leaf Gutters

Gutter guards are a great addition to any home gutter system. Here’s a look at all of the pros of having leaf guards installed on your gutters.

  • Clean gutters less frequently. Gutters need to be cleaned regularly in order to function properly, but ladders and cleaning equipment can be cumbersome and time-consuming. Gutter guards eliminate a significant amount of cleaning time by blocking leaves and other debris from entering your gutters.
    However, remember that most leaf guards don’t wholly eliminate cleaning and maintenance. You’ll still need to get up there every now and again to remove the debris from the guards themselves. But it will significantly reduce your cleaning time and extend the amount of time between gutter cleanings.
  • Protect your home from water damage. The purpose of rain gutters is to collect the water that flows off of your roof and direct it away from your home. When gutters get clogged with leaves, dirt, branches, and other debris, the water can’t get where it’s supposed to go. This often results in water overflowing out of the gutters and running down the side of your house.
    Over time, this can cause significant damage to your home’s siding and foundation. Leaf guards help keep gutters clear so water can get where it needs to go. This ultimately protects your home from water damage.
  • Extend the life of your gutters. Most rain gutters are made of sturdy and durable materials, but they can still be susceptible to damage. Gutters may wear out prematurely when excess debris gathers inside of them, gets wet, and ultimately rots. Leaf guards can prevent rotting debris, thereby extending the life of your rain gutters.
  • They can be added to existing rain gutters. Many people believe that if they want gutter guards, they need to completely replace their rain gutters. But that’s one of the biggest benefits of leaf guards – they can be added to existing gutter systems.

Cons of Leaf Guards

Although leaf guards can be an excellent addition to any home gutter system, there are some things to consider before you take the plunge. Here’s a look at some of the less desirable parts of having gutter guards.

  • Cheap options aren’t the best options. There are several options for gutter guards, and the prices can vary significantly. Many homeowners are drawn to less expensive guards, thinking they’ll get all the benefits without having to spend very much money.
    Unfortunately, the cheapest options tend to be just that – cheap. They won’t last long or give you the ongoing benefits that well-made rain gutter guards will provide. Stick with high-quality options from an established gutter company with professional installation, and you’re much more likely to be satisfied with the results.
  • Small debris may still slip through. Since water still needs to be able to get through, it’s impossible for gutter guards to completely block out all debris. Small items like pine needles, seeds, and dirt may still slip through the cracks.
  • They’re not maintenance-free. Gutter guards will significantly cut down on cleanings, but that doesn’t mean they’re completely maintenance-free. You should still expect to clean your gutters and guards every three to five years or more frequently for brush and foam gutter guards.
  • DIY installation may void your roof’s warranty. Some gutter guards are installed in the fascia or underneath the shingles, which may void some roof warranties. We don’t recommend installing gutter guards yourself, but if you do, be sure to check with the shingle manufacturer before you start. Having your guards installed by a professional rain gutter company is much safer.

M & M Gutters & Exteriors Offers the Best Solutions For Your Gutters

Your home is one of the most significant purchases you will ever make, and it’s essential to protect it from rain and storm damage. That’s why M & M Gutters & Exteriors is here to help. A leaf filter can go a long way in protecting your home from water damage, and we offer several different types. These include wire mesh leaf gutters, Gutter RX leaf guards, and Leaf X leaf solutions.

We provide several options of superior rain gutters in addition to leaf guards, including copper, box round, k-style, and custom box gutters.
We have installed thousands of gutter systems on homes across Northern Utah, including Lehi, Salt Lake City, Park City, Ogden, and more. We offer superior service to new construction, remodels, apartments, and commercial buildings. We also provide siding installation and repair, leaf guards, and ice melt systems. Contact us today for an estimate!

title: What is an Ice Melting System? - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: ice melting systems are growing in popularity. Learn about ice melting systems with a comprehensive guide from M&M Gutters, ensuring a safer home environment.
h1: What is an Ice Melting System?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Ice melting systems, also referred to as snow melting systems, are becoming increasingly popular in more homes and businesses. They are a cost-effective and convenient method of automatically clearing ice and snow from surfaces such as driveways, parking areas, emergency access areas, and sidewalks. These systems are essential to your home because they eliminate the need for labor-intensive snow removal, shoveling, and salting. Liability due to personal injuries and damage to surfaces is also decreased when you invest in an ice melting system.

Benefits of an Ice Melting System

Here are some reasons why your home or business needs an ice melting system:

  • Ice melting systems can be paired with alternative energy sources such as solar, geothermal, and waste heat. They might even be able to operate cost-free.
  • They help comply with Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) regulations and reduce liability claims.
  • The life of your paved surfaces will be extended.
  • Conserves gas and prevents pollution by eliminating the need for plows and snow blowers.
  • Keeps your interior floors cleaner by eliminating ice and snow that gets tracked inside your home.

Take advantage of alternative heat sources such as biomass, geothermal, or waste heat from within a structure for a virtually cost-free option.

How Does an Ice Melting System Work?

An efficient ice melting system detects snow/ice though inground sensors and heats the affected surface using pipes that are embedded in concrete, asphalt, or sand. This circulates a warm fluid, which in turn melts the snow and keeps the area clear at all times.

How Will an Ice Melting System Prevent Damage to my Home?

Excessive ice and snow will cause significant issues to your home’s exterior. Your home’s rain gutters, roof, and siding of your home are all subject to damage. Unfortunately, Utah residents are more prone to this damage because of the state’s winter conditions. Ice dams are the primary cause of leaking and roof damage, which creates even more complex issues for your home’s exterior.

An ice dam is a ridge of ice that forms at the edge of a roof and prevents melting snow (water) from draining off the roof. Water that backs up behind the dam can leak into a home and cause damage to walls, ceilings, insulation, and other areas. The dam grows as it is fed by melting snow above it.

Sometimes ensuring that your rain gutter is free from debris isn’t enough to prevent ice dams from forming. When ice builds up in the rain gutter, it not only builds up and over the rain gutter, (which then forms dangerous icicles) but it backs up and sneaks under the shingles on the roof; this will harm your home.

Investing in an ice melting system prevents icicles and ice dams from forming in the first place. M&M Gutters has you covered. Our self-regulating heat tape automatically adjusts its power output to accommodate to changes in outside air temperature. Contact M&M Gutters today and treat your home to a quality ice melting system.

title: What is ASTM D226? A Comprehensive Look at Roofing Felt Standards - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
meta: Explore ASTM D226 roofing felt standards. Discover #15 vs #30 types, proper installation, and ensure your roof's weather protection.
h1: What is ASTM D226? A Comprehensive Look at Roofing Felt Standards
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
What is ASTM D226 and Why Does it Matter for Your Roof?

For a quick answer, ASTM D226 is the industry standard that sets specifications for asphalt-saturated organic felt. This felt is used as an underlayment in roofing and waterproofing systems. It ensures the material meets specific quality and performance requirements for protecting your home.

  • What it is: An ASTM standard for asphalt-saturated organic felt.
  • Purpose: Defines quality and performance for roofing underlayment.
  • Types Covered: Type I (commonly called #15 felt) and Type II (commonly called #30 felt).
  • Application: Used in built-up roofs and waterproofing systems.

When you think about your roof, you probably picture shingles or tiles. But there’s a vital layer underneath that helps protect your home from the elements: the underlayment. This often-overlooked component acts as a crucial barrier. It shields your home from rain, wind, and moisture, even if your main roofing material gets damaged.

One key material used for this underlayment is roofing felt. To make sure this felt does its job well, the construction industry relies on standards. These standards ensure quality and consistent performance. One of the most important is ASTM D226. This standard covers asphalt-saturated organic felts, which are widely used in roofing and waterproofing applications. Understanding ASTM D226 means understanding a foundational part of your roof’s defense system.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors. With over 30 years serving Utah homeowners, our team specializes in roofing, siding, and exterior home improvements, ensuring every project meets the highest standards, including those set by ASTM D226. This guide will help you understand why these standards are so important for your home.

At its core, ASTM D226 is a standard specification developed by ASTM International, a global organization that creates and publishes voluntary consensus technical standards for a wide range of materials, products, systems, and services. For roofing, its primary purpose is to define the requirements for asphalt-saturated organic felt, ensuring that these materials perform reliably as underlayment in roofing and waterproofing systems.

Imagine a world without standards—every manufacturer would produce roofing felt differently, leading to unpredictable quality and performance. ASTM D226 eliminates this uncertainty by providing a common benchmark. It specifies the physical properties and performance characteristics that the felt must meet, ensuring quality assurance across the industry. This means that when we install an ASTM D226 compliant felt on your roof in Salt Lake City, we know it meets rigorous requirements for durability and protection.

This standard covers asphalt-saturated organic felts, which can come with or without perforations. These felts are primarily intended for two critical applications:

  1. Built-Up Roofs (BUR): Here, the felt is used with asphalts that conform to ASTM Specification D312/D312M. BUR systems are known for their multi-layered protection, and the felt forms a crucial part of this robust assembly.
  2. Waterproofing Systems: For waterproofing applications, the felt is used with asphalts that conform to ASTM Specification D449/D449M. This ensures a tight, water-resistant barrier, vital for protecting foundations and other vulnerable building elements.

Beyond just physical barriers, ASTM D226 felt plays a role in the breathability of your roof. Products like TRI-BUILT® #15 & #30 ASTM D226 Organic Felt are specifically designed to allow air vapor to transmit through, while simultaneously preventing water from entering. This creates a “breathable membrane” effect. Why is this important, especially in Utah’s varied climate? It helps prevent moisture buildup within the roof structure, which can lead to wood rot, mold, and premature aging of your roofing materials. By allowing trapped moisture to escape, it contributes to the overall health and longevity of your roof system, protecting your investment for years to come.

While our article focuses on ASTM D226, it’s worth noting that ASTM International develops a vast array of standards for material testing across various industries. For instance, other ASTM standards mentioned in the broader context of material testing include:

  • ASTM D2974: For determining the water content by mass of soil, rock, and similar materials.
  • ASTM D4643, D4944, D4959: These offer less time-consuming alternatives for determining water content in materials.
  • ASTM D2726: Used for determining the bulk specific gravity and density of non-absorptive compacted bituminous mixtures.
  • ASTM D2166: Specifies the test method for the unconfined compressive strength of cohesive soil.

These examples illustrate the comprehensive nature of ASTM standards, ensuring material quality and performance from the ground up, even if they aren’t directly testing ASTM D226 felt.

The Manufacturing Process

The creation of ASTM D226 compliant felt starts with an organic felt base. This base is typically made from a single thickness of dry felt, often incorporating recycled fibers. For example, some #15 ASTM D226 Felt Underlayment products boast being made of 100% recycled fiber sourced from old corrugated cardboard. This commitment to recycling is a positive step towards sustainable building practices.

Once the organic felt base is formed, the magic happens through the asphalt saturation process. The dry felt is thoroughly saturated with an asphaltic saturant. This process imbues the felt with its water-resistant properties and gives it the flexibility and durability required for roofing applications. This saturation is what transforms a simple felt into a robust underlayment capable of performing its essential role.

As mentioned earlier, some modern ASTM D226 felts are engineered to be breathable membranes. This means that while they effectively keep liquid water out, they allow water vapor to pass through. This crucial feature helps to prevent moisture from becoming trapped within the roof assembly, which is vital for preventing issues like wood rot and extending the lifespan of your roof.

Compliance and Approvals

For materials used in construction, especially those protecting your home, compliance with standards and official approvals are non-negotiable. ASTM D226 felt is no exception. Beyond merely meeting the ASTM standard, many products undergo further scrutiny and receive additional certifications from reputable organizations.

For example, you’ll often see ASTM D226 felt products mentioning approvals from entities like Underwriters Laboratories (UL). UL is an independent safety science company that tests and certifies products, ensuring they meet specific safety and performance criteria, particularly concerning fire resistance.

In regions with stringent building codes, such as Florida, products might also carry specific regional approvals. G.A.P. ASTM 30 D226 Type 2, for instance, is a Florida Building Code Approved product (FL # 2894.5) and Miami Dade Approved. While we’re in Utah, this highlights the level of scrutiny and regional compliance that high-quality roofing materials can achieve, reinforcing their reliability. These rigorous checks ensure that the roofing materials and types we use on your home are dependable and safe, no matter where you are.

The Two Types of ASTM D226 Felt: #15 vs. #30

When we talk about ASTM D226 felt, we’re usually referring to one of two main types, distinguished primarily by their weight and thickness. These are commonly known as #15 felt and #30 felt. Understanding the differences between these two is key to selecting the right underlayment for your specific roofing project.

  • Type I is commonly called No. 15 asphalt felt.
  • Type II is commonly called No. 30 asphalt felt.

The “No. 15” and “No. 30” historically referred to the weight per 100 square feet of the felt, though actual weights can vary slightly today while still meeting the standard. The primary differences lie in their material composition, coverage, weight, and ultimately, their performance and ideal applications.

Let’s break down their key specifications:

FeatureASTM D226 Type I (#15 Felt)ASTM D226 Type II (#30 Felt)
Common NameNo. 15 Asphalt FeltNo. 30 Asphalt Felt
Approx. WeightLighter (historically 15 lbs/100 sq ft)Heavier (historically 30 lbs/100 sq ft)
Coverage432 sq. ft. per roll (e.g., 36″ x 144′)216 sq. ft. per roll (e.g., 36″ x 72′)
Saturated MassMin. 11.5 lb/100 sfMin. 26.0 lb/100 sf
Breaking StrengthMin. 30/15 lbf/in (Machine Direction/Cross Direction)Min. 40/20 lbf/in (Machine Direction/Cross Direction)
CompositionOrganic felt, asphalt saturated, often recycled fibersOrganic felt, asphalt saturated, often recycled fibers
Best UseLight to moderate duty, residential, temporary protectionHeavy duty, commercial, high-wind areas, longer exposure

Key Characteristics of ASTM D226 Type I (#15 Felt)

The ASTM D226 Type I, or No. 15 asphalt felt, is your go-to for standard residential roofing projects. It’s the lighter of the two options, making it easier to handle and install.

One of its significant advantages is its coverage. A single roll of #15 felt typically covers about 432 square feet. This means fewer rolls to buy and fewer seams to deal with during installation, which can be a plus for smaller or simpler roofs. Its minimum saturated mass is 11.5 pounds per 100 square feet, and it boasts a breaking strength of at least 30/15 lbf/in (machine direction/cross direction). This provides adequate protection for many applications.

We often recommend #15 felt as an excellent underlayment for steep-slope roofing systems like asphalt shingles, wood shakes, and tiles. It provides that essential secondary layer of protection against moisture, contributing to the longevity of your roof system, whether you’re considering metal roof vs shingles for your Salt Lake City home. It’s a reliable choice for typical homes in Utah, offering good value and performance.

Key Characteristics of ASTM D226 Type II (#30 Felt)

When you need something more robust, ASTM D226 Type II, or No. 30 asphalt felt, steps up to the plate. This is the heavier, more durable option, designed for applications demanding extra protection and strength.

While a roll of #30 felt covers less area—typically 216 square feet—its increased weight and thickness translate directly into improved performance. With a minimum saturated mass of 26.0 pounds per 100 square feet and a breaking strength of at least 40/20 lbf/in, it offers superior tear resistance and puncture protection during installation and throughout its lifespan. This increased tensile strength makes it particularly well-suited for high-wind areas or roofs that might experience more foot traffic during construction.

For commercial applications or residential roofs that require heavy-duty underlayment, #30 felt is often the preferred choice. Its added robustness offers a greater margin of safety against the elements. If you’re wondering about the lifespan of a flat roof in Utah, incorporating a durable underlayment like #30 felt can contribute significantly to its overall resilience and longevity. It provides a more substantial barrier, capable of withstanding harsher conditions and providing extended protection.

Applications and Best Practices for Installation

ASTM D226 felt is a versatile material, primarily used as a secondary weather barrier in roofing systems. Its role is critical: to protect your home from wind-driven rain and other environmental elements that might penetrate the primary roofing material. This makes it an excellent choice as an underlayment for steep-slope roofing types such as shingles, wood shakes, and tiles, which are common across Salt Lake City and Northern Utah.

But its utility isn’t limited to just under shingles. This robust felt can also be installed under various other building materials, providing an extra layer of moisture protection for applications like siding (stucco, aluminum, vinyl, wood) and even some flooring systems. This versatility underscores why it’s such a staple in our exterior remodeling projects.

Roof Deck Preparation and Ventilation

Proper installation begins long before the felt rolls out. The roof deck must be carefully prepared to ensure the underlayment performs optimally and lasts for years. This means:

  • Clean and Dry Deck: The surface must be free of debris, dirt, and moisture.
  • Repairing Damaged Sheathing: Any decayed, rotting, rusted, or broken materials on the roof deck must be removed and replaced. We can’t build a strong roof on a weak foundation!
  • Securing Loose Nails: All loose nails should be removed and the deck should be secured to the framing with correct fasteners.
  • OSB Sheathing Considerations: If new OSB sheathing is being used, it’s crucial to leave appropriate expansion gaps (e.g., 1/8″ at end joints, 3/16″ at side joints, always verifying with the manufacturer). Pre-conditioning new OSB can also help minimize expansion and contraction issues down the line.

Beyond the deck itself, adequate ventilation under the roof deck is absolutely paramount, especially when considering how to prevent roof damage during Utah winters. Proper attic ventilation (ridge vents, soffit vents, etc.) prevents humidity buildup. Without it, excessive moisture can lead to:

  • Wrinkling and ridging of the underlayment.
  • Buckling of the primary roofing materials.
  • Wood rot in the roof deck and structural components.
  • Premature aging of your entire roofing system.

In Utah’s climate, where we experience both cold winters and hot summers, managing moisture and heat is critical. Good ventilation ensures that your roof can “breathe,” promoting a healthy, long-lasting system.

Application and Fastening your ASTM D226 Felt

Once the deck is prepped, the careful application of ASTM D226 felt begins. Here’s how we ensure a professional, secure installation:

  1. Horizontal Installation: The felt is run horizontally across the roof, starting from the bottom edge (the eaves). This allows gravity to help shed water over the overlaps, preventing moisture intrusion.
  2. Eave to Ridge: Each course of felt is laid, working your way up the roof towards the ridge. The felt should align so its edge covers up to the rake and eaves but doesn’t extend over the sides.
  3. Initial Securing: To hold it in place while unrolling, we’ll typically install about 5 nails in a 2-inch square pattern in the top right corner of the felt.
  4. Unrolling and Alignment: The felt is unrolled approximately halfway across the roof (20-25 feet). We pull it until it’s tight and smooth, eliminating any wrinkles. Once aligned straight and flat, a nail is hammered in the top corner.
  5. Nailing Pattern: We then install nails every 6-8 inches across the top, center, and bottom of the felt to secure it thoroughly. This robust fastening prevents the felt from shifting or tearing.
  6. Overlap Requirements: Subsequent layers of felt require a 2-inch overlap with the course below. We use the guidelines printed on the felt itself for precise alignment. At the ridge, the last layer should overlap by approximately 8 inches and be securely nailed.
  7. Wrinkle Prevention: Sometimes, wrinkles can still appear. If they do, they are slit with a utility knife, nailed flat, and then sealed with flashing cement. This meticulous attention to detail is crucial for preventing potential leak points. How to find a roof leak can be a frustrating experience, and proper underlayment installation is key to avoiding it.

Specific Requirements for Roofing Nails: The choice and application of fasteners are critical. We follow recommendations from organizations like the National Roofing Contractors Association (NRCA). For ASTM D226 felt, this means using:

  • Type: 11-gauge or 12-gauge galvanized steel roofing nails.
  • Head: Low-profile, smooth, flat heads.
  • Shank: Barbed or deformed shanks for superior holding power.
  • Length: Nails must be long enough to penetrate through all layers of felt and the roof deck, or at least 1 inch into wood decks. This ensures a secure attachment that won’t pull out under wind stress.

Safety is always our priority. Before handling any product, we read all product safety data sheets and container labels to ensure the well-being of our team and your property.

Frequently Asked Questions about ASTM D226 Felt

We often get questions from homeowners about the specifics of roofing felt. Here are some of the most common ones regarding ASTM D226 felt:

Is ASTM D226 felt waterproof or water-resistant?

This is a great question! ASTM D226 felt is primarily water-resistant, not fully waterproof. Think of it as a highly effective secondary barrier. Its asphalt saturation allows it to shed water efficiently, preventing moisture from penetrating the roof deck if the primary roofing material (like shingles) is compromised or during heavy rain and wind.

However, it’s not designed to be a standalone, permanent waterproofing layer. It relies on the primary roofing material for the main protection. If exposed to the elements for extended periods, or if submerged in water, it will eventually allow moisture to pass. Its role is to provide a critical backup defense, giving your roof system an extra layer of resilience.

Can I use #15 felt for all roofing applications?

While #15 ASTM D226 felt is suitable for many standard residential roofing applications, it’s not a one-size-fits-all solution. For typical steep-slope roofs with asphalt shingles in areas with moderate weather, #15 felt often provides adequate protection.

However, there are situations where #30 ASTM D226 felt is the better, or even required, choice:

  • Local Building Codes: Some local building codes, especially in high-wind zones or areas prone to severe weather, may mandate the use of #30 felt due to its superior tear strength and weight. Always check with your local Salt Lake City building department!
  • Roof Slope Considerations: While both can be used on steep slopes, roofs with lower pitches might benefit from the added protection of #30 felt.
  • Heavy-Duty Applications: For commercial buildings, roofs that might experience more foot traffic during maintenance, or under heavier primary roofing materials like certain tiles, the increased durability of #30 felt is often preferred.
  • Extended Exposure: If there’s a chance the underlayment might be exposed to weather for a longer period during construction, #30 felt offers greater resilience.

We carefully assess your specific roof, local conditions, and building codes to recommend the appropriate type of ASTM D226 felt for your project.

How long can roofing felt be exposed to the sun and weather?

ASTM D226 felt is designed for temporary exposure to the elements during the roofing process, not long-term. While its asphalt saturation provides water resistance, prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun will cause it to degrade.

Manufacturers typically specify a maximum exposure time, which can range from a few days to a couple of weeks, depending on the product and local conditions. After this period, the felt can become brittle, lose its protective qualities, and even tear easily.

It’s crucial that the primary roofing material (shingles, tiles, etc.) is installed over the felt as soon as possible after the felt is laid. This protects the underlayment from UV degradation and ensures its long-term performance as a secondary barrier. If your roofing project faces delays, we take steps to protect any exposed felt, or we’ll replace it if it’s been exposed beyond its recommended limits to ensure the integrity of your roof system.

Conclusion: Trust the Experts for Your Utah Roofing Needs

Understanding standards like ASTM D226 might seem technical, but it’s fundamentally about ensuring the quality and longevity of your roof. This foundational underlayment plays an invisible yet vital role in protecting your home from the harsh realities of weather, from heavy rains to strong winds, a common occurrence in our beautiful Utah landscape.

Choosing ASTM D226 compliant materials means you’re investing in a product that has met rigorous industry standards for performance and durability. However, even the highest quality materials are only as good as their installation. Proper preparation of the roof deck, meticulous application techniques, and correct fastening are all critical steps that ensure your underlayment can effectively do its job as a secondary weather barrier. This attention to detail is what helps prevent common causes of roof leaks in Salt Lake City and extends the life of your entire roofing system.

For professional roofing installation and exterior remodeling in the Salt Lake City area, Salt Lake County, Utah County, Summit County, Tooele County, Davis County, Weber County, and throughout Northern Utah, trust the 30+ years of experience at M&M Gutters & Exteriors. We’re committed to using high-quality materials and applying expert craftsmanship to every project, ensuring your home is protected for years to come.

title: What Is Roofing Felt and What Is Its Purpose? - M&M Gutters
meta: Many components of roofing systems often go unnoticed, one of which is roofing felt. What is roof felt, and what part does it play in installation?
h1: What Is Roofing Felt and What Is Its Purpose?
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
Many components of roofing systems often go unnoticed, one of which is roofing felt. What is roof felt, and what part does it play in installation? Read on to learn more about the purpose of roofing felt, the many different types, and why every home can benefit from this roofing material.

What Is Roofing Felt?

Roof felt is a versatile material used in roofing. It has many names, including roofing paper, roofing tar paper, or roof underlayment. This material is made from a combination of asphalt and either fiberglass or organic fibers. Roofing contractors install roof felt between the roof deck and shingles. It has become an essential part of installations.

Is Roof Felt Waterproof?

While not entirely waterproof, the primary purpose of roof felt is to repel moisture and prevent it from entering your home. It’s designed to repel water rather than absorb it, so it can break down if wet for too long.

What Does Roofing Felt Do?

So, what is roof felt used for? Besides preventing water from entering your home, roofing felt is used as:

  • Ice repellant. Because it repels water, roof felt can offer extra protection against ice dams and damage.
  • Extra weather protection. Felt roofing paper protects against various weather conditions, such as wind and UV rays. It enhances your roof’s overall durability.
  • Additional fire protection. Roofing felt contributes to meeting a Class A fire rating when used with shingles.
  • Assists with look and uniformity. Besides protection, roof felt also creates a smooth and uniform surface for your shingles, helping them lay flat and uniform.

What Is Roofing Felt Made Of?

There are a few types of materials roof felt can be made from, such as

  • Felt. Traditional roofing paper is made from organic fiberglass with an asphalt coating.
  • Synthetic. Synthetic roofing underlayment comes from polypropylene or other synthetic ingredients.
  • Wood structural panel and underlayment. This type of roof felt is for use under wood shingles or shakes.
  • Peel-and-stick underlayment. This self-adhesive roofing felt offers easy installation.

What Are the Different Weight Options for Roofing Felt?

Felt paper for roofing comes in two weight options. These options are based on the weight of 100 square feet of material. It indicates the felt’s thickness and durability.

15 pounds

This lighter roofing paper is best for roofs that can’t handle larger amounts of weight or have a steep pitch where water can run off easily. It’s more suitable for areas with mild weather conditions and provides basic protection, but it may be more susceptible to wear and tear.

30 pounds

Roof felt that weighs 30 pounds is for more heavy-duty projects. It’s ideal for areas with harsh weather conditions where additional protection is needed. It offers more resistance to wear and tear but adds more weight and stress to the roof.

Does My Roof Need Roofing Felt?

Roofing paper isn’t always used, but it has many benefits that outweigh the costs. It acts as a backup layer of weather protection under your shingles, ultimately extending the life of your roof deck.

title: Home Improvement: What is the Average Cost of Rain Gutters?
meta: The cost of rain gutters can vary significantly depending on the size of your home and the type of gutters you choose. There are plenty of inexpensive options
h1: What Is the Average Cost of Rain Gutters?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
The cost of rain gutters can vary significantly depending on the size of your home and the type of gutters you choose. There are plenty of inexpensive options, and you can save even more money by installing them yourself. But there’s a good chance you won’t be happy with the result and will wish you’d gone with a professional installation of better-quality gutters from the get-go.

Here’s a look at how much it might cost to install new rain gutters on an average home.

National Average Rain Gutter Cost

Nationwide, the average cost of rain gutters is $1,125. It may cost as much as $8,000 for some homes and as little as $800 for others. The actual cost of installing new gutters on your home may be higher or lower than the national average, depending on several factors. Those cost-altering factors include:

  • location,
  • size and type of the home,
  • type of rain gutter material,
  • rain gutter style,
  • and nature of the installation.

For example, installing rain gutters on a 4-story home is likely to cost more than an installation on a rambler; this may be true even if both houses have the same size roof. There may also be additional charges for replacing existing gutters rather than adding gutters to a new building that hasn’t had them before — this is because there is extra work associated with removing old gutters, repairing fascia, and disposing of materials.

Cost of Rain Gutters by Material

Rain gutters come in various materials, and some cost a lot more than others. There are also differences in performance and durability, so consider those when choosing a material. The cheapest options may not save you any money if you have to replace them in a few years. Here’s an overview of the different types of rain gutter materials and how they stack up cost-wise.

  • Aluminum – Aluminum rain gutters tend to be the most popular. That’s because the material is lightweight, so it’s easier to attach and isn’t prone to sagging. Aluminum gutters also come in various colors, which are resistant to corrosion and keep looking nice for longer.

They’re one of the less expensive options and generally cost around $3 per linear foot for the materials. They aren’t the most durable gutters because they are prone to dents which can decrease performance over time.

  • Steel – Steel gutters are generally made of galvanized steel coated in a zinc layer. This makes them strong and durable, but they tend to rust. Steel gutters may also be coated in both aluminum and zinc to remain durable and help with the rust problem.

They are similar in cost to aluminum gutters at about $3 per linear foot. The downside? Installation costs on steel gutters tend to be quite a bit more expensive because they are so heavy. They are also prone to sagging and pulling away from the roof with time due to their weight.

  • Zinc – Zinc gutters are less common, but there’s a lot to love about them. They are one of the most durable gutter materials and commonly last in the ballpark of 100 years. Zinc is fully recyclable, too, so they’re an eco-friendly choice. Additionally, zinc gutters add a significant amount of curb appeal. More people don’t choose them because they cost anywhere from $10 to $25 per linear foot.
  • Copper – Copper shares a lot of the upsides of zinc. It’s recyclable, durable, and attractive. Copper gutters oxidize to form a beautiful patina over time that protects the gutters from rust. This material is often installed on older homes and buildings. But, like zinc, copper gutters are on the high end of the price scale. You can expect to pay $10 to $12 per linear foot for copper gutters, not including installation costs.
  • Vinyl – Vinyl is easily the least expensive gutter material. You can find vinyl gutters for as little as $2 per linear square foot. And while vinyl gutters might look nice initially, they have the shortest life span and will need to be replaced frequently. They become brittle in direct sunlight and break easily, decreasing their functionality and harming the physical appearance of your home. But they are cheap and extremely easy to match to a home’s vinyl siding, which is why so many people choose them.

Installation Costs

The cost of the rain gutter materials is only part of the total cost of getting new gutters. Installation costs also need to be considered. Installation costs around the nation may be as low as $1,000 or as high as $5,000. You can expect to pay between $7 and $33 per linear foot of installed gutters in addition to the material costs.

Downspouts are another additional cost that many people tend to overlook. Downspouts are required every 40 feet, so most homes need at least four downspouts. These are typically made of the same material as the gutters you choose.

All in all, with materials and installation costs, you can expect to pay between $1,000 and $5,000 for new gutters on your house. You might be tempted to install them yourselves. But it’s well worth the cost of hiring a professional gutter company to handle the installation for you so you can have the peace of mind that it’s done correctly and your home is protected.

Upgrade Your Rain Gutters With M&M Gutters & Exteriors

As you can see, the cost of rain gutters can vary significantly. So if you’re ready to have beautiful and high-performing gutters installed on your home, the M&M Gutters & Exteriors experts are here to help. Our knowledgeable and professional team has decades of industry experience, and no job is too big or little for us.

Our skilled crew is fully licensed and insured. We are committed to delivering high-quality gutters, siding, and service to homes and businesses in Salt Lake, Weber, Davis, Utah, and Summit counties in Utah. Contact us for all your gutter repairs, custom gutter systems, and other gutter needs. We also specialize in siding installation, roofing, and windows.

title: What Is the Best Ice Melting System? | M&M Gutters
meta: Ice and snow can wreak havoc on your roof and gutters and create injury. Learn why using an ice melting system is a must to protect friends and family.
h1: What is the Best Ice Melting System?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Welcome to winter, where ice and snow can wreak havoc on your roof and gutters and create hazardous conditions when the water pools on your porch or the driveway. Learn why using an ice melting system is a must to protect friends and family.

The Best Ice Melting System

A quality melting system prevents the buildup of snow and ice on roofs and gutters. It involves using a heating element (heating cable) that increases conductivity to produce heat, which is best for harsh winters. There are two types of melting systems: Electric snowmelt and hydronic snowmelt. See more about them.

Types of Melting Systems

There are normally just two melting systems available for use in exterior slabs on grade. Both rely on four key components to transfer the slab surface into a whole radiant heat source; they are:

  • An embedded heating element in the slab
  • A power source
  • Sensors to detect outdoor air temps and moisture
  • A controller to tie everything together (heating element, sensors, and power source)

Electric Snowmelt Systems

These types of snowmelt systems use three components: heating cable, a control unit, and an activation device. Because the heating cable can sustain harsh conditions, it’s suitable for outdoor use. The control units are usually wall-mounted control panels and vary by technology using line and load terminal blocks, relays, activation terminals, along with monitoring electronics.

Heat tapes self regulate and prevent icicles and ice dams from forming in the first place. They deliver the exact amount of heat needed to accommodate any changes in outside air temperature. There are 120 V and 240 V systems, depending on someone’s needs. When the temps drop, the polymer increases conductivity, which then produces heat. When the temps rise, it decreases conductivity for less heat.

Hydronic Snowmelt Systems

With this type of heating system, the heating element is a closed-loop tubing or modular thermapanel system; it’s typically made of a flexible polymer or synthetic rubber that moves around a mixture of hot water and antifreeze—propylene glycol. The fluid is warmed to 61℉ to 140℉ that warms surrounding concrete/asphalt, thus melting snow and ice. Like electric snowmelt systems, hydronic systems can be installed in or beneath the base material (sand).

Why Use Ice Melting Systems?

Melting systems have risen in popularity for both residential and commercial use and are used for:

  • Convenience – Installing snowmelt systems in sidewalks, driveways, steps, and patios eliminate the need for shoveling.
  • To target trouble spots – If you can’t afford to install the system in all your exterior concrete slabs, you can use them only where snow and ice pose a problem.
  • To reduce snow removal costs and liability – business owners may use the system in parking lots, car washes, walkways, and loading ramps to reduce snowplowing costs and to prevent accidents.it’s way cheaper than paying lawyer fees and a possible litigation settlement, as well.

title: Exterior Siding: What Is the Easiest Siding To Install?
meta: If you’re wondering what house siding is the easiest to install, here’s a look at some of the most common types of siding and what installation is required.
h1: What Is the Easiest Siding To Install?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Installing most types of siding is fairly straightforward; it just takes a well-planned layout and the right tools for the job.

House siding trends change just like home interior trends do. Masonite siding was all the rage in the ‘80s and ‘90s, and that gave way to the vinyl and stucco craze of the early 2000s. Today, tongue and groove siding is found on most new builds.

These ever-changing trends leave many people wanting to update their siding to something more current. So, if you’re wondering what house siding is the easiest to install, here’s a look at some of the most common types of siding and what the installation process looks like for each.

Start With a Plan

It’s extremely important to form a solid plan before you get started with any home exterior project. Siding can be tricky, especially when you try to wing it. Lay out your pieces of siding before you start any work, and if you notice that there will be any areas that don’t work as well, try to make sure that section is on a less visible part of the house.

Allow plenty of time to plan and lay out your project so that the actual installation process goes as smoothly as possible. Better yet, call a professional to help you achieve the siding of your dreams.

Tongue-and-Groove Siding

Tongue-and-groove siding is exactly what it sounds like — siding that has tongues and grooves on either side so it slides together to make a seamless panel. The panels over and under-lap each other to snap together and cover your home’s exterior.

Installing this type of siding isn’t extremely difficult, but it’s not appropriate for all areas. If you live in a very wet environment, you might want to pick a different material for your home’s exterior since tongue-and-groove doesn’t offer as much protection from the elements.

Vinyl Siding

Vinyl is widely known as one of the cheapest and easiest siding materials to install on a home’s exterior. It’s easy to cut and apply and doesn’t need to be painted. But while the actual application is simple, preparing your home for vinyl siding is a lot more work.

To prepare for vinyl siding application, you first need to check all of your boards and trim. Replace anything rotten and tighten any loose boards. Next, scrape away any old caulk from windows and doors. Remove any exterior fixtures that will interfere with installation, and ensure no landscaping will get in the way.

Furring strips are generally required when installing new vinyl siding to your home’s exterior; this helps account for any uneven walls and makes the vinyl look even, smooth, and finished rather than uneven and irregular.

Board and Batten Siding

Board and batten have become extremely popular in home exteriors in recent years. This style gives off a farmhouse vibe but can work well on any home. The actual installation process for this exterior isn’t too difficult as long as it is well planned out.

Before you cut any boards or punch any nails, it’s important to think about what kind of spacing you want in between the boards and what type of wood you’re going to use. Not all boards are the same size. Generally, the boards are made using 1×10 boards and 1×3 battens, but you can use different sizes.

The type of wood you choose can also impact how difficult or easy the installation will be. Cedar is the most common wood used for board and batten because it’s somewhat soft and easy to nail to your house and seal without cracking. Harder woods, like pine, are prone to cracking and are much more difficult to install.

It’s also important to prepare your home’s exterior before you apply this type of siding. You can install the boards and battens onto solid plywood or oriented strand board sheathing. A home without solid sheathing or plywood will need furring strips to be applied horizontally before starting on the actual siding application.

Siding Shingles

Shingles are fairly new to the siding game, but they offer a rustic charm to any home. Shingles are frequently applied under the eaves of houses rather than to the entire exterior, but plenty of homes use shingles across the outside. This type of siding is commonly referred to as “cedar shake” siding.

Installing shingles to the sides of your house can be very time-consuming because they need to be applied in three layers for maximum protection against the elements. This process means you will likely need to buy more shingles than you expect. Many homeowners choose to paint or stain their singles before installing them, which adds a huge amount of time and work to the process.

Do you like the look of shingles on a home exterior but aren’t up for installing it yourself? This job — along with all siding jobs — is best left to experienced professionals.

But, if you’re set on doing it yourself, another option both homeowners and professionals have is to use shingle panels. These are large panels of plywood covered in shingles, so you can apply the entire panel to your home at once rather than installing each individual shingle — this can save a ton of time, but it might be more difficult to paint or stain the shingles on the panels.

title: What Is the Lifespan of a Flat Roof in Utah? - M&M Gutters & Exteriors
h1: What Is the Lifespan of a Flat Roof in Utah?
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
If you own a home or maintain a commercial building with a flat roof in Utah, you’ve probably wondered at some point, “How long does a flat roof last?” Flat roofs have a distinct appearance, performance, and materials compared to sloped roofs. They also have a minimal slope, typically less than 10 degrees, and are great for outdoor areas.

This article aims to answer your questions and provide information on the types of flat roofs available, as well as their advantages and disadvantages, to help you decide whether a flat roof is a good idea for your home.

What Is Metal Roofing?

A metal roof is made of metal materials, like aluminum, copper, tin, or zinc, and functions like any other type of roof to provide protection. You can get a metal roof in several styles, colors, and finishes to create a unique look on your home.

How Long Does a Flat Roof Last?

Many factors contribute to the lifespan of a flat roof. Everything from weather to the materials used to the type of roof installed impacts the lifespan. On average, expect about 20 years of life from a flat roof. Still, extenuating weather circumstances can make the lifespan shorter. The materials used and regular maintenance of a flat roof can increase the lifespan, though no one can precisely predict how long a roof will last.

How Does Utah’s Weather and Climate Impact Flat Roofs?

Utah’s weather and climate impact the lifespan of flat roofs. Snowy winters in Logan and Park City can leave standing water on roofs if they don’t drain properly, leading to leaks and water damage inside the building. Bright, sunny, dry days in St. George and Moab can eventually lead to roof blistering and cracking due to the high amounts of UV radiation Utah receives. A cracked roof can leak when it rains, causing water damage.

Flat Roof vs. Angled Roofs

Flat and angled roofs (pitched or sloped roofs) have distinct characteristics. They are suitable for different architectural styles and climates. Here are some critical differences between flat roofs and angled roofs:

Flat Roofs:

  • Aesthetic appeal: Flat roofs often have a modern and minimalistic aesthetic.
    Use of space: Flat roofs can create additional living space for things like rooftop gardens, solar equipment, or outdoor living space.
  • Cost: Flat roofs are typically more cost-effective compared to angled roofs because they are easier to design and build.
  • Maintenance: Maintenance of flat roofs is generally easier as access is straightforward. However, proper drainage is crucial to avoid ponding water.
  • Weather sensitivity: Flat roofs are more susceptible to water pooling, and proper drainage is essential. They may also face challenges with snow accumulation.

Angled Roofs:

  • Aesthetic variety: Angled roofs offer various design possibilities and are commonly associated with traditional, classic, or regional architectural styles.
  • Water drainage: Angled roofs naturally facilitate water runoff, making them less prone to water-related issues such as ponding or leaks.
  • Snow shedding: In regions with heavy snowfall, angled roofs allow for snow shedding, reducing the risk of excessive snow load on the roof.
  • Weather adaptability: Angled roofs are generally better suited to various weather conditions, including heavy rainfall and snow.

What Type of Roofing is Best for a Flat Roof?

The best type of roofing for a flat roof depends on your climate, budget, and how long you want it to last. EPDM, TPO, and PVC are among the most popular flat roof materials because of their durability, water resistance, and energy efficiency. However, traditional options like BUR and modified bitumen also offer solid protection at a lower cost.

If you’re looking for longevity or energy performance, certain materials clearly stand out.

BUR

A BUR (built-up roof) has layers of bitumen and fabrics, which often have several layers. These provide great insulation and protection against weather events. On average, a BUR roof will last approximately 15 years before signs of wear and tear begin to show.

EPDM

Ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) is made from rubber membranes, providing optimal insulation and protection. If your area is prone to hailstorms, this is the preferred roofing material to protect your home. The approximate longevity of an EPDM roof is 20 years.

PVC

A polyvinyl chloride (PVC) roof is a top consideration when longevity is essential. Compared to other options, a PVC flat roof is extremely water-resistant, meaning it provides excellent protection for your home. This type of flat roof can last around 30 years if it is well-built and maintained correctly.

TPO

Thermoplastic polyolefin (TPO) is a newer flat roof material. These single-ply roofs have a membrane that uses polymer fillers to increase strength and durability. These are great roofs to protect against UV rays. A typical lifespan of TPO roofs is between 15 and 30 years.

Spray-On Coating

A three-layer sprayed-on polyurethane roof coating can provide excellent protection from wind and damaging UV rays. This option can be substantially more expensive than other roof types. When properly maintained, however, this roof type can last for decades.

Modified Bitumen

These roofs are incredibly durable and low-maintenance. A modified bitumen roof provides adequate protection from the elements and is entirely water resistant. When installed correctly, this roof can last around 20 years.

Pros of Flat Roofs

There are several advantages of flat roofs compared to pitched roofs. These advantages include:

  • Affordability: Due to easier flat roof installation, they are more affordable than traditional pitched roofs
  • Easy to clean: Flat roofs are easier to clean and maintain than pitched roofs. They are safer for the person on the roof, too!
  • Versatility: One of the main benefits of a flat roof is that it’s extremely versatile. Grow a garden when you lack yard space, add a fire pit, create a relaxation area, and more.
  • Energy efficiency: Flat roofs are more energy-efficient due to the material used and the lack of attic space they create.
  • Equipment availability: A flat roof offers more usable space, making it easier to install HVAC units and solar panels.

Cons of Flat Roofs

While flat roofs offer many advantages, there are also disadvantages to consider. Here are a few to help you decide if a flat roof is the right choice for your home:

  • Water pooling: Water doesn’t drain easily from a flat roof, resulting in long-term damage.
  • Water leakage: Heavy rain and melted snow can often be found in the cracks of a flat roof.
  • Weather sensitivity: Flat roofs are commonly exposed to UV rays and heavy snowfall, which can cause cracks and drainage issues.
  • Shorter lifespan: Some flat roofs have shorter lifespans and require regular maintenance.

What Are the Risks Associated With Flat Roofs?

The risks associated with flat roofs are mostly related to weather. Since the roof is flat instead of sloped, it is easier for water to gather. This standing water can cause puddles if the roof doesn’t drain properly, which can eventually seep into the roof and cause water damage to the property. If you notice any discoloration spots on your ceiling, it could indicate that there is an undetected leak somewhere in your roof.

Warm temperatures can eventually cause flat roofs to crack and blister. When this occurs, it may be time for a roof repair or replacement.

How to Extend the Lifespan of Your Flat Roof

Proper cleaning and regular maintenance and inspections will help extend your flat roof’s lifespan.

What Is the Cost of a Flat Roof Installation?

The cost of flat roof installation will vary greatly depending on the material used and the size of the project. A roof assessment will provide more information about the best roof for your needs and the associated costs.

What Is the Cheapest Way to Cover a Flat Roof?

EDPM, a synthetic rubber, is one of the most affordable ways to cover a flat roof, especially in sunny Utah climates like Ogden, Layton, or Salt Lake City. This roofing material is lightweight and can last up to 20 years with proper care.

Are Flat Roofs a Good Idea?

Ultimately, flat roofs can be a cost-effective and practical roofing option, especially for modern homes and commercial buildings. They typically cost less to build than pitched roofs, offer easier access for roof maintenance, and create usable space for features like solar panels, HVAC systems, or rooftop patios.

That said, flat roofs aren’t ideal for every climate. They require proper drainage systems and regular upkeep to prevent issues like standing water and roof leaks. Their lifespan can also be shorter than that of sloped roofing systems, especially in areas with heavy rainfall or snow.

Flat roofs work best for:

  • Dry or mild climates like Utah’s
  • Modern or minimalist architecture
  • Buildings that benefit from extra roof space

Not sure if a flat roof is right for you? Talk to a roofing contractor to explore the best flat roofing systems for your location, structure, and budget.

h1: What Types of Rain Gutters Are There?
author: Nathan Nuttall
content:
Whether you’re building a new house or remodeling your old one, rain gutters are an essential part of the process. They serve several crucial functions in your home. Most importantly, they direct water away from your home’s foundation to prevent flooding, cracking, and severe foundation damage. Gutters also help protect rainwater from dripping down your home’s exterior, which can cause excess wear and even erode your siding.

If you think you might prefer your home’s appearance without gutters, think again. There are three main styles that gutters come in: k-style, half-round, and box style. Each of these styles comes in a variety of materials, so with the help of a qualified professional, you can pick and choose a gutter that will complement the look of your home while also keeping it safe from water damage. Here’s an in-depth look at the different types and materials of gutters.

K-Style Gutters

Next time you’re walking through the neighborhood, pay attention to the rain gutters on each house. Most of the systems you’ll see are k-style. Despite their name, they aren’t shaped like the letter K. They look more like crown molding that you might find in a modern home. The back of these gutters is totally flat so that they can be easily installed around the trim around your roof. Industry-standard gutters are five inches, but they can also be purchased in a six-inch size if they need to hold more water.

There are many reasons k-style gutters are so standard. First of all, they are typically the cheapest option available. They also have rigid construction, so they’re more durable than half-round gutters, and they’re easy to install. If you live in a wet area, you might like k-style gutters because they can hold more water than other styles. For all the benefits, though, there are some downsides. This style is more likely to clog than other types and is also prone to corrosion.

Half-Round Gutters

Half-round gutters are more common in older homes and historic buildings. They look exactly like they sound, with half a round pipe on the bottom and an open top. Since they are round, installing these gutters is a little more complicated. Brackets are first installed around the edge of the roof, and then the gutters are set in and secured.

This type of gutter is more expensive than the k-style, and they can’t handle as much rain. But that doesn’t mean that they don’t have their benefits. Half-round gutters’ biggest pros are that the entirely smooth interior helps prevent clogging and is easier to clean.

Box Style Gutters

The least popular gutter on the market is box style. They’re very rare in homes and are most often used in commercial or industrial buildings. That’s because they are oversized to handle a large amount of water. The bigger the roof, the more water your gutters need to be able to hold. So it makes sense that large roofs like those in commercial buildings would need larger gutters. They come in seven, eight, and even ten-inch sizes.

Box-style gutters must be installed simultaneously with the roof because they slip underneath the shingles. So if you’re remodeling, they’re not typically an option unless you’re getting a new roof.

Rain Gutter Materials

The gutters and downspouts on your house are all made from the same materials, and it’s most likely aluminum, copper, vinyl, or galvanized steel. You can get k-style and half-round gutters in any of those materials, but box gutters usually only come in copper or aluminum. Most can be painted to match your home or commercial building’s exterior. Let’s break down each material and look at its pros and cons.

Aluminum

Aluminum is an extremely common material for gutters because it is lightweight, making it easy to install. It’s also inexpensive, is resistant to rust and corrosion, and comes in several color options. The one downside of aluminum gutters is that they can warp easily when temperatures fluctuate because they are so lightweight.

Copper

There’s a reason copper is so desirable in things like piping and gutters. It’s a highly durable metal and adds sophistication and elegance to your home. Over time, copper gutters develop a desirable patina. There’s a lot to love about copper gutters, but that doesn’t mean it’s all sunshine and roses. They are typically the most expensive option, and they are heavy, so installation is more complicated. Their weight also causes them to pull loose more often than lighter materials like aluminum.

Vinyl

Vinyl is creeping its way into many home construction items, primarily because it’s cheap and easy to work with. It’s also waterproof, which is a must for gutters. Surprisingly, there aren’t a lot of color options for vinyl gutters. Most come in white only. The cheap material also breaks and bends easily, so they aren’t as durable as some of the other materials.

Galvanized Steel

If you’re looking for gutters that can handle heavy rains and snow, galvanized steel is right up your alley. They’re extremely strong and durable, but that comes with a price. They are one of the more expensive options, they’re super heavy, and they are prone to rust.

Keep Your Home Safe With M & M Gutters & Exteriors

Your home is one of the most significant purchases you will ever make, and it’s essential to protect it from rain and storm damage. That’s why M & M Gutters & Exteriors is here to help. We offer several different types of rain gutters, including copper, box round, k-style, and custom box gutters.

We have installed thousands of gutter systems on homes across Northern Utah, including Lehi, Salt Lake City, Park City, Ogden, and more. We offer superior service to new construction, remodels, apartments, and even commercial buildings. We also offer siding installation and repair, leaf guards, and ice melt systems. Contact us today for an estimate!

h1: What’s the Damage? Estimating Your Rain Gutter Installation Cost
author: M&M Gutters & Exteriors
content:
How Much Does It Cost to Have Rain Gutters Installed?

The cost to have rain gutters installed typically falls between $2,624 and $4,723 for a typical single-family home in 2026, or roughly $10 to $16 per linear foot installed.

Here’s a quick-reference breakdown:

Cost TypeTypical Range (2026)
Per linear foot (installed)$10.41 – $15.77
Average home (full system)$2,624 – $4,723
Budget range$628 – $1,732
Premium or complex installs$5,000 – $12,500+

Your final number depends on a few key variables:

  • Material — vinyl and aluminum are the most affordable; copper costs the most
  • Linear footage — most homes need 150 to 250 linear feet
  • Home height — two-story homes add $1 to $3 per foot in labor
  • Roof complexity — steep pitches, multiple gables, and valleys increase costs
  • Add-ons — downspouts, gutter guards, and fascia repairs all affect the total

Read on and we’ll walk through every factor in detail so you can build a realistic budget before calling anyone.

I’m Nathan Nuttall from M&M Gutters & Exteriors, and with over 30 years of hands-on experience helping Utah homeowners understand the cost to have rain gutters installed, I know what drives prices up — and where you can save without cutting corners. Let’s break it all down clearly so you can make a confident, informed decision.

Simple guide to cost to have rain gutters installed terms:

  • 5 inch gutters price
  • average cost to install rain gutters

Breaking Down the Average Cost to Have Rain Gutters Installed

When we talk about the national average for gutter projects, we often see a range of $2,623.82 to $4,722.87. However, averages can be a bit like weather forecasts in Salt Lake City—they give you a general idea, but the reality on your specific street might be different. Most homeowners across the country pay around $4,000 to replace gutters on a typical single-family home, usually falling within the $2,800 to $5,200 range.

The biggest driver of this number is linear footage. Most homes require between 150 and 250 linear feet of gutters. If you have a small ranch-style home, you might only need 100 feet; a sprawling two-story estate in Summit County could easily exceed 300 feet.

To give you a clearer picture, we’ve broken down the estimated What is the Average Cost of Rain Gutters? based on common system sizes:

System Size (Linear Feet)Estimated Cost Range (Installed)
100 Linear Feet$1,041 – $1,577
150 Linear Feet$1,561 – $2,365
200 Linear Feet$2,082 – $3,154
250 Linear Feet$2,602 – $3,942

Calculating the Cost to Have Rain Gutters Installed per Linear Foot

As of January 2026, the benchmark cost to have rain gutters installed per linear foot sits between $10.41 and $15.77. This figure isn’t just for the metal or plastic hanging off your roof; it covers a blend of local material delivery, worksite preparation, protection of your landscaping, and the skilled labor required for a precise installation.

Labor generally accounts for 10% to 50% of the total project cost. For a basic installation, you are paying for the layout, fabrication (especially with seamless systems), securing the gutters to rafters, and ensuring a proper drainage slope. If the pitch is off by even a fraction of an inch, you’ll end up with pooling water and a very expensive mosquito nursery. You can find more detail on these breakdowns in this guide on Gutter Installation Cost: How Much Homeowners Typically Spend.

Regional Variations in the Cost to Have Rain Gutters Installed

In our neck of the woods—specifically Salt Lake City and the surrounding Northern Utah areas—pricing can vary from the national baseline. Utah’s average often trends slightly higher due to the demand for durable materials that can handle heavy snow loads and freeze-thaw cycles. Recent data suggests Utah averages can range from $18.56 to $22.55 per linear foot for high-quality professional installs.

Factors like labor availability in Davis or Weber County and the cost of shipping specialized materials to the Mountain West play a role. Furthermore, homes in high-rainfall or heavy-snow locations may require wider 6-inch gutters instead of the standard 5-inch, which can increase the system capacity and the price by up to 50%. You can compare these local trends with broader How Much Does Gutter Installation Cost? [2026 Data].

Material Selection: Balancing Durability and Price

Choosing the right material is where you decide between a short-term fix and a long-term investment. In our Rain Gutter Materials Guide, we emphasize that the “cheapest” option isn’t always the best value over 20 years.

Aluminum and Vinyl Options

Aluminum is the heavyweight champion of the gutter world—not in actual weight, but in popularity. It is rust-resistant, lightweight, and comes in over 20 prefinished colors. You can expect to pay between $6 and $14 per linear foot installed for aluminum. It lasts a solid 20 to 30 years and handles the Utah climate quite well.

Vinyl (PVC) is the most budget-friendly choice, often starting as low as $3 to $7 per linear foot. While it won’t rust, it has a shorter lifespan of 10 to 15 years. In extreme cold, like we see in Summit County, vinyl can become brittle and crack. If you’re debating between the two, check out our comparison: Vinyl vs Aluminum Gutters: Which One is Best?.

Premium Steel and Copper Systems

For those looking for maximum strength or high-end aesthetics, steel and copper are the go-to choices.

  • Galvanized Steel: Costing $8 to $26 per foot, these are incredibly strong but require maintenance to prevent rust.
  • Copper: This is the “luxury” option, ranging from $25 to $50+ per foot. Copper gutters can last 50 to 100 years and develop a beautiful green patina over time. They are often required for historic homes in Salt Lake City to maintain architectural integrity.
  • Zinc: Similar to copper, zinc is self-sealing and can last over 80 years, though it carries a premium price tag of $40 to $50 per foot.

Factors That Shift Your Installation Estimate

Every home is unique, and a “simple” 2,000-square-foot house might cost more than a 3,000-square-foot one if the roof looks like a game of Tetris. If you notice 5 Signs Your Home Needs a New Gutter System, you’ll want to consider these cost-shifting factors:

  1. Home Height: Working on a two-story home is more dangerous and time-consuming. Expect a premium of $1 to $3 extra per linear foot for any work above the first floor.
  2. Roof Pitch and Complexity: Steep roofs require specialized “spike and ferrule” hangers or extra brackets to ensure the gutters stay put. Multiple gables, valleys, and “bump-outs” increase the number of mitered corners and joints, which adds to labor time.
  3. Accessibility: If our crew has to navigate tight spaces, overgrown landscaping, or complex architectural features, the labor hours will climb.

Additional Components and Hidden Fees

The gutters themselves are only part of the system. To get the water safely away from your foundation, you’ll need these essentials:

  • Downspouts: These cost between $5 and $40 per linear foot depending on material. We typically recommend one downspout for every 20 to 30 feet of gutter.
  • Gutter Guards: These are a popular add-on in 2026, costing between $7 and $20 per foot. They significantly reduce maintenance by keeping leaves and debris out.
  • Fascia Repair: If your old gutters were leaking, the wood behind them (the fascia board) might be rotted. Replacing this costs $5 to $12 per linear foot.
  • Removal and Disposal: Taking down your old, heavy gutters and hauling them to the dump usually adds $1 to $3 per linear foot to the bill.

Seamless vs. Sectional: Comparing Long-Term Value

If you’ve spent any time researching the cost to have rain gutters installed, you’ve likely seen the term “seamless.”

Performance and ROI

Sectional gutters are sold in pieces at big-box stores. They are cheaper upfront but have seams every 10 to 20 feet. Every seam is a potential leak point. Over time, the sealant in these joints fails, leading to drips that can rot your siding or flood your basement.

Seamless gutters are custom-fabricated on-site using a specialized machine that “spits out” a single continuous piece of metal tailored to the exact length of your roofline. Because they only have joints at the corners and downspouts, the risk of leaks is drastically reduced. While they cost more initially ($6 to $28 per foot depending on material), the maintenance savings and increased home value make them a far better investment. Learn more about the tech in What are Seamless Rain Gutters? and see Why You Shouldn’t Install Your Rain Gutters Yourself.

Frequently Asked Questions about Gutter Installation

Is it cheaper to install gutters yourself?

Technically, yes, you save on labor. However, we’ve spent 30 years fixing DIY “saves” that ended up costing double. DIY risks include:

  • Safety: Ladder falls are one of the leading causes of home improvement injuries.
  • Pitch Issues: If the gutters aren’t sloped perfectly toward the downspouts, water will pool, leading to rust and clogs.
  • Warranty: Most professional materials come with warranties that are voided if not installed by a licensed pro. Avoid these Common Gutter Installation Mistakes by hiring a team with the right equipment.

How long does a typical gutter installation take?

For most homes in Salt Lake or Utah County, we can complete a full installation in a single day. If there is extensive fascia repair needed or if the home is particularly large and complex, it might stretch into a second day. Weather is the only real wild card—we can’t install in high winds or heavy snow for safety reasons.

How often should new gutters be replaced?

This depends entirely on the material and how well you maintain them.

  • Vinyl: 10–15 years
  • Aluminum: 20–30 years
  • Galvanized Steel: 20 years
  • Copper/Zinc: 50–100 years Regular cleaning (twice a year) can add years to these estimates. For a deeper dive, read How Long Do Rain Gutters Last?.

Conclusion

Investing in high-quality rain gutters is one of the most cost-effective ways to protect your home’s foundation, landscaping, and roof. While the cost to have rain gutters installed can vary based on your home’s size and the materials you choose, the price of not having them—foundation cracks, mold, and flooded basements—is much higher.

At M&M Gutters & Exteriors, we bring over 30 years of experience to every home in Northern Utah, from Tooele to Summit County. We don’t just guess at your costs; we use advanced 3D visualization technology like HOVER to give you an exact, transparent estimate of your project.

Ready to see what a new system will look like on your home? Explore our Rain Gutters Installation services and let’s get your home protected for the next 30 years.
